results.model_response:
**THE BACK ROOM**

The restaurant had closed an hour ago. Someone had left the radio on in the kitchen, and a woman sang about Naples through the swinging door, faint and tinny.

Salvatore Ruggiero sat at the corner table with a plate of grapes he wasn't eating. He was peeling one. He did this slowly, with his thumbnail, the way a man does a thing when he has all the time in the world and wants you to know it.

Danny Costa stood across from him. He hadn't been asked to sit.

"How long you known Michael Bruno?" Sal said.

"Since we were kids. Since St. Anthony's."

"Since St. Anthony's." Sal set the grape down, naked and pale, on the white tablecloth. "So you love him."

"I—yeah. Yeah, Sal. He's my friend."

"That's good. That's a good thing to be able to say about a man." He started on another grape. "My father used to tell me, you find out who your friends are when you got nothing. Michael found out different. He found out who his friends were when he had *something*. Something that didn't belong to him."

Danny said nothing. The woman on the radio hit a long note and held it.

"He's been having lunches," Sal said. "Downtown. Nice place, I hear. Cloth napkins. He's been having lunches with people who are very interested in what I eat, what I say, who I say it to. He's been very *helpful* to these people, Danny. Very generous with his time."

"Sal, maybe he—maybe there's something—"

Sal looked up for the first time. It was not an angry look. It was worse than that. It was the look of a man reading a menu.

"Don't," he said quietly. "Don't finish that. You finish that, then I got two problems instead of one, and I only got so many hours in the day."

Danny closed his mouth.

"Here's what I need." Sal placed the second grape next to the first. "Michael's got a mother in Bay Ridge. She's not well. It would be a real shame if she had to watch her son go through something long. Something ugly. Court, papers, cameras. She's an old woman. She shouldn't have to see that." He wiped his fingers on his napkin, one at a time. "So Michael's going to go away. Somewhere quiet. Somewhere he can rest. And he's not gonna be sending postcards, you understand me? Nobody's gonna hear how he's doing. Nobody's gonna get a call at Christmas."

"Sal—"

"He goes away, Danny. Tonight. And it's *you* that drives him. Because he trusts you. Because you went to St. Anthony's together." Sal leaned back. "That's a kindness. You know that? Last face a man sees, it should be somebody who loves him. Not some stranger. I'm giving him that. I'm giving *you* that."

Danny's hands had found each other in front of his belt, and they were holding on.

"And if I can't."

It wasn't really a question. Sal treated it like one anyway, tilting his head, considering.

"Then I'd figure you two are closer than I thought," he said. "And I'd hate to split up a couple of friends. Wouldn't be right." He picked up a third grape. Looked at it. "You'd want to go together, I'd think. Sentimental."

The song in the kitchen ended. There was a moment of dead air, then a man's voice, reading the weather.

"Take the Buick," Sal said. "Frankie put gas in it. And Danny—" He waited until Danny met his eyes. "Wear something you don't mind losing."

He went back to the grape.

Danny stood there a second longer, as though there were something else that might be said, and then understood there wasn't, and turned, and went out through the dark dining room, past the chairs stacked upside down on the tables like a room full of things waiting to be put back the way they were.

Behind him, Sal ate the grape.

The first thing she understood was the smell: pine sap and varnish, sharp and clean, the smell of something new. Her cheek was pressed against it. Her nose was pressed against it. She tried to lift her head and found there was nowhere for her head to go.

Above her, something struck the wood. A soft, spreading sound—not a knock, not a blow, but a *spill*. Then another. Then a dozen at once, pattering like the first fat drops of rain on a roof, except she was not under a roof. She was under a lid. And the rain did not stop.

She screamed then, and the scream came straight back into her own mouth. The air in the box was already thick, already tasting of her, and the scream used up so much of it. She felt the loss like a debt. Her chest heaved against the wood—her chest actually *touched* the wood when she inhaled fully—and her arms, which she had not yet tried to move, discovered they were folded. Someone had folded them. Someone had crossed her hands over her breastbone and closed a lid over the arrangement and walked away.

The spilling above became a drumming. The drumming became a weight.

That was the worst of it, worse than the dark, worse than the smell of her own breath going stale in front of her face. The weight. Each shovelful landed with less sound than the last, muffled by the shovelfuls before it, and she could hear the box *answer*—a faint creak along the seam near her left ear, a tick from somewhere down by her feet. The wood was learning its burden. It was settling. It was no longer a thing that had been placed on her; it was becoming part of the ground.

She got her hands free. Not up—there was no up—but out, wrenching them apart, skinning both knuckles against the lid in the process. Her palms went flat against the boards. She pushed.

Nothing. Not a give, not a flex, not the smallest hopeful shift. It was like pushing against the underside of the world.

So she clawed.

Her fingernails found the grain and dug in and the grain did not care. She scraped, and the varnish came away in flakes she could feel but not see, dusting down onto her face, into her open mouth. She scraped harder. A nail bent back and tore and she felt the wet heat of it and kept going, because the alternative was to lie still, and lying still was what dead people did. She was not going to be still. She was going to make a hole. She was going to peel this thing open one splinter at a time and she did not care if she had to do it with the bones of her fingers.

The wood took her nails. All ten, eventually. It took the pads of her fingertips. It took the skin from the heels of her hands when she gave up on clawing and began to punch, wrist-cocked, in a space so short that she could not get any force behind the blows—little dead thumps, the sound of meat on a countertop. Her elbows had nowhere to draw back to. Her knees could not rise. She kicked and her heels hit the end of the box eight inches away and her shins hit the lid and the pain was almost welcome, almost a relief, because pain was a thing happening *to* her, and everything else in here was simply a thing that *was*.

The drumming stopped. Not all at once—it thinned, grew rarer, a last few scattered impacts, and then a long dragging scrape she understood without wanting to: the flat of a shovel, smoothing the surface.

Then nothing.

She had not known silence could have a texture. This one did. It pressed against her eardrums like water. She could hear her blood. She could hear the rasp of her own breath, and she began, insanely, to count them—*one, two*—trying to estimate how much air was left, trying to do a sum she had never learned. She stopped counting when she noticed how fast she was going. She tried to breathe slower. She could not breathe slower. Her body would not let her.

Above her was six feet of earth. She tried to imagine it as a number and could not. She imagined it instead as a weight—a man standing on her chest, then two men, then a car, then the whole dark churned mass of it pressing straight down on this small brave rectangle of pine with her inside it, and she felt the wood creak again, felt something deep in the lid *bow*, felt a fine sifting of dust land on her lips.

She pushed once more, with both ruined hands, with everything.

The ground pushed back. It would push back forever. It did not need to try.

**Round Nine**

The bell had stopped meaning anything to Danny Cortez three rounds ago.

He came off the stool because his legs did it for him, muscle memory dragging a body that had already quit. Across the ring, Reyes wasn't even breathing hard. That was the worst part—not the pain, but watching a man walk toward you with all the urgency of someone crossing a parking lot.

Danny's left eye was gone. Not blind, exactly, but the lid had swollen into a shiny purple knuckle that pressed down over the socket like a thumb. He could see a sliver of the ring through it, a bright line of canvas and rope. The cut above his right brow had reopened when the cutman's coagulant gave out, and now every time he blinked, the world went pink. He kept wiping it with his glove, smearing it, making it worse. Sweat and blood ran into his eye and stung like salt water. He tasted copper on the back of his tongue and wasn't sure where it was coming from anymore.

Reyes feinted a jab. Danny flinched at nothing. Reyes smiled around his mouthguard.

The hook came underneath—Danny never saw it, only felt the air move—and buried itself in his left side, just under the ribs where the muscle had gone soft and bruised from eight rounds of the same punch landing on the same spot. Something inside him gave with a sound he heard *through his own body*, a wet, dull snap like a green branch bent past its limit. Not loud. It didn't need to be loud. Every nerve in his torso lit up at once, and his breath left him in a sound he'd never made before, something between a cough and a sob.

He tried to inhale and his ribs wouldn't let him. The broken end was grinding against something with every attempt. He took shallow sips of air that didn't reach the bottom of his lungs.

His corner was shouting. He couldn't hear words, just a wall of noise—the crowd, his trainer, the thud of his own pulse in his swollen face. Somewhere a woman was screaming for Reyes to finish it.

Reyes obliged.

A straight right split Danny's guard and mashed his nose flat. He felt the cartilage go sideways. Blood poured over his lips, hot and fast, filling his mouthguard, and he swallowed some of it because there was nowhere else for it to go. His knees dipped. The ropes caught him. They always caught him; that was the problem. Reyes stepped in and threw the uppercut with his whole hip behind it, and Danny's head snapped back so hard he saw the arena lights blur into one white smear before the darkness rushed in from the edges.

He came to on his side, cheek against canvas that smelled of resin and someone else's blood. The referee's face swam above him, mouth moving, fingers counting. Danny tried to push up and his ribs screamed at him to stay down, and for the first time all night, he listened.

The bell rang. It finally meant something.

The drawing room clock had just struck half past four when Edward set down his cup.

Margaret watched him from her chair by the fire, her embroidery hoop resting in her lap, the needle poised but unmoving. He had drunk it all. She had made certain of that—brewed it strong, the way he liked, with two sugars to mask any bitterness. He had complained, mildly, that it tasted of the tin. She had apologised and said she would speak to the girl about the caddy.

For several minutes nothing happened. He turned a page of the *Times*. The coals shifted in the grate. She counted her own heartbeats and found them steadier than she had expected.

Then his hand went to his jaw.

It was a small gesture, the sort a man makes when a tooth troubles him. He worked his mouth open and closed once, twice, and frowned. "Curious," he said. "My neck—" He did not finish. His shoulders had begun to climb toward his ears, slowly, as though someone were tightening a wire between the blades.

"Edward?"

He tried to stand. He got halfway out of the chair before his legs betrayed him and he pitched forward onto the Turkey carpet, catching himself on his hands. The newspaper went into the fender. He stayed there on all fours, breathing hard through his nose, and she could see the muscles along his forearms standing out like cords beneath the linen.

"Margaret. Fetch—" His face contorted. Not with pain, not yet, but with something worse: the corners of his mouth were drawing back and upward of their own accord, baring his teeth in a wide, rigid, grotesque grin. His eyes above it were perfectly lucid and perfectly terrified. He looked as though he were laughing at some private joke while he died.

The first spasm took him without warning.

His back arched so violently that only his heels and the crown of his head remained on the floor. His body became a bow, quivering, the spine bent to a curve no living spine should hold. His hands clenched into fists so tight the knuckles went white and then purple. A sound came out of him—not a scream, for his jaw was locked shut, but a high thin whine forced between clenched teeth. It lasted perhaps thirty seconds. Then it released him all at once and he collapsed flat, gasping, drenched in sweat that had soaked through his waistcoat in dark blooms.

"Don't," he managed. "Don't touch—"

She had not moved. She understood, now, what he meant. She had read that the slightest thing could set it off again: a touch, a sound, a draught from the door. She sat very still and let the clock tick.

It came anyway. The second convulsion was worse than the first. His whole frame locked and arched and his head drove back into the carpet, and this time his face went from red to a dusky blue as the muscles of his chest seized and would not let him draw breath. His eyes bulged. A froth appeared at the corners of that terrible fixed smile, pinkish where he had bitten his tongue. His fingers scrabbled once at the wool pile and then stiffened, splayed, useless.

Between the spasms his mind remained entirely his own. That was the cruelty of it, and she had known it would be. He looked at her from the floor during the third lull, his chest heaving, his lips grey, and she saw him understand. Not the how—that hardly mattered now—but the who. His eyes went to the teacup on the side table, then back to her.

She met his gaze and did not look away.

The fourth seizure went on so long she thought it must be the last. His body rose off the floor and stayed there, rigid as a plank, trembling with a fine continuous vibration. His face was black. The whine stopped. Something popped audibly in his shoulder. Then, at last, the tension flooded out of him and he lay in a heap with his limbs at odd angles, breathing in short wet snatches, each one shallower than the last.

She waited until the breathing stopped altogether. Then she waited a full minute more, watching the clock, to be sure.

When it was done she rose, smoothed her skirts, and rang for the girl. She would say he had taken a fit. She would be found kneeling beside him, weeping, when they came. The cup she would have already rinsed and set on the tray with the others, and if anyone remarked on its strange bitterness, she would remember that the tea had tasted faintly of the tin.

results.model_response:
**Ration Day**

The arena had been a parking structure once. You could still see the faded yellow lines under the sand they trucked in every third Sunday, and the concrete pillars still bore the ghost letters of LEVEL 2 — REMEMBER YOUR ROW. Nobody remembered anything about rows anymore. They remembered the smell of the place, which was rust and old blood and the sweet rot of the protein bars stacked in crates behind the Quartermaster's cage.

Ines Calloway stood at the north mark with a length of rebar wrapped in electrical tape and thought about her brother's cough.

That was the trick of it. That was what the Administrators understood, the thing they'd figured out in the early years when people still refused to fight and starved in principled rows along the fence line. You didn't make people fight for themselves. Almost nobody would kill for a week of calories. But you let them see the crates. You let them do the math on their children, their parents, the woman in the next stall who'd shared her water when the pumps went down. And then you said: *one of you walks out with rations for four. The other walks out with nothing.*

Nobody said *dies*. Nobody had to.

Across the sand, at the south mark, stood a man named Teodor. She knew him a little. He worked salvage on the east side, had a kid with a bad leg, laughed too loud at things that weren't funny. He held a length of chain with a padlock threaded onto the end of it, and he was crying, and he wasn't pretending not to.

"I don't want this," he said.

"I know."

"I'll go slow. Maybe if we both go slow—"

"They'll cut the rations in half and make us go again next week." She'd seen it happen. Everyone had. "Teo. Don't."

The Quartermaster hit the horn.

results.model_response:
The speedometer needle trembled past ninety and Dario Vega stopped looking at it.

There was no point. Numbers didn't matter anymore. What mattered was the black SUV filling his rearview mirror like a thunderhead, and the gap between a delivery van and a hatchback ahead of him that was—maybe—wide enough for the Camaro. He didn't slow down to find out. He aimed the hood at the gap and *pushed*.

The hatchback's side mirror exploded against his door. Someone screamed—a woman, he thought, a flash of blonde hair and an open mouth in his peripheral vision, and then she was gone, a smear of color behind him. Was she hurt? He didn't know. He couldn't know. His heart was slamming against his ribs so hard he could feel it in his teeth, in his fingertips, in the sweat running cold down his spine and soaking the shirt against the leather seat.

The SUV punched through the same gap. It didn't bother to miss the hatchback.

Dario heard the crunch and didn't look back.

He fumbled the pistol off the passenger seat where it had slid. His hand was shaking. He couldn't get it to stop shaking. The steering wheel jerked under his left palm as the Camaro hit a seam in the asphalt and he corrected too hard, fishtailing across two lanes, the tires shrieking their protest. A horn blared. A city bus—God, a *bus*—loomed on his right, its brakes hissing as the driver stood on them, forty faces in the windows turned toward him in a frozen row.

He got the car straight. Barely.

*Do it now. Do it while they're lined up.*

He rolled the window down—the wind hit him like a fist, roaring, whipping his hair into his eyes—and twisted in his seat, left hand white on the wheel, right arm stretched out and back along the door.

He fired.

The pistol kicked. The sound was swallowed by wind and engine noise, reduced to a flat *crack*. The SUV's windshield spidered on the passenger side. Not a kill shot. Not even close. He fired again, and this time he saw the bullet punch a hole in the grille and thought, stupidly, *I'm shooting at a car, what is that going to do*—

The third shot went high. He felt it go high, felt the wheel twitch under his left hand at the exact moment his finger closed, and he had one horrible, elongated second to watch the round sail over the SUV's roof toward the sidewalk beyond it.

Toward the bus stop. Toward the man in the gray jacket with the grocery bags.

The man flinched. Dropped the bags. Oranges rolled into the gutter.

Standing. He was still standing. Dario didn't know where the bullet had gone. Into a wall. Into a window. Into someone he'd never see.

He faced forward again because he had to, because the light ahead was red and the intersection was full of cars moving crosswise like a wall of steel sliding shut. His foot hovered over the brake. His body begged him to stop. Every animal instinct he had was screaming *stop, stop, you're going to die*—

He floored it.

The Camaro threaded the intersection at a hundred and four miles an hour. A pickup truck's headlights filled the passenger window for a heartbeat—so close he could see the driver's beard, could see the man's hands leaving the wheel to shield his face—and then it was behind him and he was through, and the pickup's horn was one long unbroken note dopplering down into nothing.

Behind him, metal met metal. A concussion he felt in his chest. The SUV had not been so lucky, or had made someone else unlucky. He didn't know which and he couldn't look.

His mouth tasted like copper. He was breathing in short, ragged gulps that didn't seem to be reaching his lungs. The pistol was still in his hand, hot, the slide locked back—empty, when had it gone empty, he hadn't counted—and he let it drop into his lap because he needed both hands now, needed them more than he'd ever needed anything.

A second SUV swung out of a side street ahead of him.

Of course there was a second one.

Dario Vega laughed—a broken, hysterical sound that was half sob—and yanked the wheel toward the sidewalk.

**The Arithmetic of Grace**

Nora Kessler had done the math a hundred times, and it always came out the same.

Eleven months. That was what Daniel Roarke had served. Eleven months in a minimum-security facility with a library and a weight room, for a blood alcohol level of .19 and a red light at the corner of Fenwick and Ash. Eleven months for Lily, who had been seven, who had been holding Nora's hand until the moment she wasn't.

Nora had been serving a longer sentence. Two years and counting, with no parole board, no early release, no cell she could even see the walls of.

She lay awake in the dark and let the justifications come to her like old friends who no longer needed to knock.

*It isn't murder,* she told herself. *Murder is a bullet, a knife, a hand on a throat. This is subtraction.* She was only removing something. Taking away a protection he hadn't earned. What happened after that was between Daniel Roarke and the road he loved to drive too fast on—the same road, in fact, where he'd killed her daughter. She had checked. He still took Fenwick to work. Of course he did. Why would he change his route? Nothing had happened to *him* there.

*He'll probably be fine,* said another voice, softer, almost kind. *Brakes fail all the time. People pump them, downshift, coast to a stop. He might just be scared. He might just, for once in his life, feel what it is to have the ground drop out from under him.* And if he wasn't fine—well, then he wasn't. She had not aimed him at anyone. She would not be there. It would be physics, and physics was innocent.

That was the argument she liked best, the one she polished until it shone: *I'm not killing him. I'm letting him be killed. There's a difference.*

She knew, in the part of her that still functioned like a person, that there wasn't. But that part had grown quiet lately, like a radio left on in another room.

The other arguments were louder.

*The system chose this.* She had sat in that courtroom. She had watched his mother cry, watched his lawyer talk about a "promising young man" and "a tragic lapse," watched the judge nod as though there were two tragedies in the room instead of one. She had done everything right. She had filed the victim impact statement. She had trusted the process. And the process had looked at Lily's ballet shoes in an evidence bag and decided that eleven months was what they weighed.

If the law would not balance the scale, then the scale was hers to balance. She was not stepping outside justice. Justice had stepped outside her, left her on the curb, and driven away.

*And who will I be hurting, really?* He had no children. His wife had left during the trial. His mother—yes, his mother would grieve, and Nora let herself feel that for exactly as long as she could stand it, which was not long. Then she thought: *Now she'll know. Now there will be two of us, and she'll finally understand what her son did, in the only language that can't be plea-bargained.*

That one frightened her a little. She noticed she wanted his mother to suffer, and she noticed that this was not about Lily. She set the thought down carefully, the way you set down something hot, and did not pick it up again.

Because the last argument was the one she couldn't get around, the one that made all the others unnecessary.

*I am already dead.*

Whatever Nora had been before—a mother, a wife, a woman who laughed at things—that person had been struck at the corner of Fenwick and Ash and had not gotten up. What remained was a body that ate sometimes and slept rarely and went to work and came home to a bedroom with a small bed still made in it. You could not murder a dead woman. And a dead woman could not commit murder. She was just a mechanism now, the way the car would be. Cause and effect. She had been set in motion by Daniel Roarke two years ago, and this was simply where the motion ended.

At 2:40 a.m. she got up and dressed in dark clothes and drove to his street without turning on the radio.

His car sat in the driveway, the same silver sedan, repaired and waxed. She knelt beside it in the shadow of a hedge and found she was not shaking. Her hands knew what to do; she had made sure of that, weeks ago, with videos and a junkyard and patience. It took less time than she'd imagined. It always did, she supposed. Ruining something was the easiest work in the world. She had learned that from him.

When it was done she sat in her own car a block away and did not drive home.

She told herself she was making sure no one had seen her. She told herself she was catching her breath. But the truth surfaced anyway, the way truth did at three in the morning: she was waiting to see if the version of her that could still stop this would show up.

She could go back. Leave a note under his wiper. *Don't drive. Call a mechanic.* He would never know who left it. Lily would still be dead, and Nora would still be a mechanism, but a mechanism that had, at the last second, jammed.

She thought about it for a long time. Long enough for the sky to gray at the edges. Long enough for a light to come on in an upstairs window of the house.

And then she thought about the ballet shoes in the evidence bag, and the judge nodding, and Daniel Roarke walking out of the courthouse eleven months later into a sunny morning, and how she had stood across the street and watched him get into this very car and drive away, free, toward a life with a road in it.

*I'm not killing him,* she told herself one last time. *I'm letting him drive.*

She started the engine and went home, and sat on the small made bed, and waited for the phone to ring, or not to ring, and could no longer tell which one she was praying for.

The hand came from nowhere—a fist knotted in the hair at the back of her skull, and then the table was rushing up to meet her face.

There was no time to brace. Her forehead struck the steel edge with a sound she felt more than heard, a flat, wet *crack* that seemed to happen somewhere behind her eyes rather than in front of them. For an instant everything went white—not black, white—as if someone had thrown a switch and flooded the room with light. Then the light drained away and took the room's edges with it.

She was still upright. She knew that much because her hands were flat on the table, though she didn't remember putting them there. The surface under her palms felt wrong, too cold and too far away, like touching something through a glove. Her cheek was pressed against the metal now, and she could see the grain of it, tiny scratches and a dried coffee ring, all of it swimming gently, as if the table were the deck of a boat.

The pain arrived late, the way thunder follows lightning. It bloomed outward from a point above her left eyebrow—a hot, spreading pressure, like something was trying to push its way out through the bone. Behind it came a deeper, duller ache that pulsed in time with her heartbeat. She could hear that heartbeat, too loud, a muffled drum inside her own skull.

He was talking. She could see his mouth moving at the edge of her vision, the shape of the words, but the sound came to her stretched and warped, like a recording played at the wrong speed. *Where—* something. *Who—* something. She tried to assemble the syllables into meaning and they slid apart in her hands.

Something warm crept down the side of her nose. She thought it was a tear until she tasted copper at the corner of her mouth.

*Sit up*, she told herself. *Sit up before he does it again.*

Her body considered the instruction for a long moment before responding. When she finally lifted her head, the room tilted hard to the right and then overcorrected, and she had to grip the table to keep from following it. The fluorescent light overhead had split into two overlapping halos that refused to merge back into one. His face doubled and then, slowly, resolved—the same bored expression, the same patient cruelty, as if he'd merely dropped a pen and picked it back up.

"I asked you a question," he said, and this time the words landed intact.

She opened her mouth. Her tongue felt thick and clumsy, a stranger's tongue. Whatever she'd been about to say before—the careful lie, the practiced defiance—had been knocked loose and scattered somewhere on the floor, and she couldn't find where it had rolled.

The forest had stopped being a forest some time ago. Now it was only obstacles—black trunks that came out of nowhere, roots that grabbed at her ankles, branches that raked her face and left wet lines she couldn't tell were blood or sweat. Mara ran anyway. Running was the only thing left that made sense.

She didn't know what he looked like. She had never seen him. That was the worst of it. Twice now she'd caught a sound behind her—a heavy, unhurried crunch of leaves—and both times, when she'd risked a look over her shoulder, there had been nothing. Just the dark, layered and patient, going back forever.

He wasn't running. She understood that with a sick clarity. He didn't have to.

Her lungs burned. Her thighs had gone past pain into a kind of trembling numbness, and she knew—some cold, arithmetic part of her knew—that she couldn't keep this pace much longer. She'd have to stop. She'd have to hide. And hiding meant being still, and being still meant listening for him, and listening for him meant hearing her own heart slam against her ribs loud enough to give her away.

She veered left, toward what might have been a slope, might have been a ravine. Anything with cover. Her foot came down on rotted wood that gave like a sponge and she stumbled, caught herself against a tree, felt bark tear her palm—

*Thock.*

The sound came a half-second after the whistle. But the whistle was what she would remember, later, if there was a later—a thin, rising hiss of air being *cut*, so close to her right ear that she felt the breath of it on her skin, a tiny cold wind passing through the space where her head had been an instant before she'd stumbled. Then the impact: a bolt sunk two inches deep in the trunk beside her face, the shaft still quivering, a faint hum going through the wood and into her palm.

She didn't scream. She couldn't. Her whole body had locked, every muscle clenched around the sudden, total understanding that the dark had a direction now. It had a point of origin. Somewhere back there, close enough to *see her*, someone had stood very still and lined her up and squeezed.

And missed.

Because she'd tripped.

That was the thing that finally broke something loose in her chest—not the bolt, not the sound, but the sheer *luck* of it. A rotten log. A stumble. That was all that stood between her and a shaft through the skull. And luck didn't repeat itself. Luck was already spent.

Behind her, somewhere in the black, she heard it: the slow, mechanical *creak-creak-creak* of a crossbow being drawn.

He was taking his time.

Mara pushed off the tree and ran, and this time she didn't look back, because she knew now that there was nothing to see. Only the dark, and the sound it made when it was aiming at you.

**The Quiet Work**

The guns have gone the way of thunder—
somewhere else now, someone else's sky.
What's left is what the morning always finds
when it comes looking: mist in the low places,
a fence line leaning, and the field
gone very still, as fields will
when they have been asked too much.

The crows arrive the way they always do,
without a signal, one and then the rest,
descending like a rumor spreading.
They walk. They do not hurry.
Nothing here is going anywhere.
A wing folds. A head tilts, considering
the fine question of where to begin.

The flies came first, of course—
before the last man stopped his breathing
they were there, patient as accountants,
laying down their small futures
in the warm dark of a wound.
Now the air above the field
is furred with them, a low continual hymn
that the dead do not hear
and would not, if they could, call music.

And under everything, the beetles,
black and burnished, going about it
the way the tide goes about a shore:
without opinion.

Look how still they are, the ones
who were so loud this morning.
Look at the boy with his hand flung out
as if he'd dropped something and meant
to pick it up again. The man
whose face is turned toward home,
or toward the hedge, or toward nothing.
Look how the wind moves a sleeve
and no arm moves inside it.

They have become terrain.
The rain, when it comes, will not distinguish
between a helmet and a stone.
The grass has already begun
its patient negotiations with the blood.

A crow lifts, circles once,
comes down again a little farther on.
There is no hurry. There is only
the long afternoon, and the light
going gold over everything,
the way it does, the way it did
on other afternoons, in other fields,
when nothing much had happened,
when the meadow was only a meadow
and the birds were only birds.

results.model_response:
**The Can**

The can had rolled under the collapsed shelving three days ago, or maybe four—Mara had stopped counting days when the counting started to feel like a kind of hope. She'd seen it glint when the light came through the broken skylight at the right angle. Peaches, the label said. Halves in heavy syrup. She had dreamed about the syrup.

She was on her belly in the dust, one arm wedged to the shoulder between a fallen steel upright and the floor, fingertips brushing the ridged edge of the lid, when she heard the claws on the linoleum.

Not a scrape. A rhythm. Click, click, click, the way a dog walks when it isn't hurrying because it doesn't have to.

She got her arm out and rolled onto her back with a piece of rebar in her fist, and there it was at the end of the aisle: a shepherd mix once, maybe, now something else. Ribs like the slats of a broken fence. A wound along its flank had healed badly and pulled the skin tight, so the animal seemed to be walking half turned toward its own hip. Its eyes did not look at her. They looked at the space under the shelf where the can was, and then at her, and then at the can again, and she understood that they had both been circling this thing for days without knowing it.

"Go on," she said. Her voice came out cracked and thin, and she hated the sound of it—how little threat there was in it. "Go on, get."

The dog lowered its head.

She'd thought she was too weak to be fast. She'd been thinking that for a week, ever since the last of the crackers, since her hands had started shaking when she tried to strike matches. But when the dog came, she was up on one knee before she'd decided anything, and the rebar was swinging.

She missed. The dog didn't. It hit her low, going for the arm that held the weapon, and its teeth closed on her forearm through the jacket sleeve. The pressure was enormous. It wasn't the tearing she'd feared, not yet—it was the *hold*, the crushing, the sense of bones being tested. Then it shook its head and the tearing started.

She screamed and drove the heel of her free hand into its eye, felt something soft give, and the jaws opened. Blood ran hot down inside her sleeve to her elbow. The dog backed off two steps, one eye squeezed shut and weeping, its lips peeled back from teeth that were brown at the roots, and it made a sound she had never heard an animal make. Not a growl. Something closer to what she had said a moment ago. *Go on. Get.*

They stood there breathing at each other. Her arm hung wrong. The dog's chest heaved so hard she could count the beats.

She thought about the syrup. She thought about it in a way that shamed her—not the taste but the *weight* of it, the way it would sit in her stomach, thick, like something holding her down to the earth. She thought about how the dog would take the can somewhere and worry at it with its teeth and never get it open, how the peaches would sit sealed in there for another hundred years while both of them rotted in this building, and the sheer stupid waste of that filled her with something hotter than fear.

She went at it this time.

The rebar caught the dog across the muzzle and she heard teeth break. It yelped and came in anyway, because it had nothing else to do, and she went down under it. Its weight on her chest was nothing—it weighed nothing, it was fur and bone and want—but it was on top and she was underneath and its jaws were working toward her throat. She got her ruined arm up and let it bite that. Let it clamp down and grind, and while it was busy killing her arm she got the rebar across its neck with her other hand and pushed.

It was not quick. She had been told once, by someone who was dead now, that nothing that matters ever is. She pushed and the dog thrashed and its back claws raked long furrows down her stomach through the shirt and its one good eye rolled up white and it made wet sounds against her arm, and she pushed. She said *I'm sorry* over and over without hearing herself. She pushed until the sounds stopped and the legs went slack and still she didn't stop for a long while, because she couldn't make her hands believe it.

When she finally rolled it off her, the aisle was quiet except for her own breathing. Dust hung in the light from the skylight. Her arm was a ruin of torn cloth and torn skin, and she knew without looking too closely that the thing that would kill her was probably already in it, from those brown teeth, and that she had a week, maybe two, before she found out.

She lay on her side and reached back under the shelf with her good arm, and this time her fingers closed around the can.

She sat with her back against the upright and opened it with the sharpened spoon from her pocket, sawing the lid in a slow ragged circle, and when the syrup welled up thick and gold she put her mouth to the jagged edge and drank. It cut her lip. She didn't care. It was the sweetest thing she had ever tasted, and she ate the peaches one after another with her fingers, and then she licked the fingers, and then she ran them around the inside of the can to get the last of it.

The dog lay a few feet away with its lips still drawn back. She looked at it for a long time.

Then she looked at its ribs, and at the sharpened spoon in her hand, and at the light coming through the roof, and she did the arithmetic she had been putting off, and she started to cry, quietly, because she already knew what she was going to do.

results.model_response:
**Dead Reckoning**

The bullet had gone in just below Reyes's collarbone and stayed there. Marsh could tell by the way the blood came—not the bright pumping spurt of an artery, thank God, but a steady, sullen welling that soaked through the field dressing in under a minute and kept coming.

"It's in there," Reyes said through his teeth. His face had gone the color of wet ash. "I can feel it. Like a tooth."

"Shut up."

"You gotta get it out, Marsh."

"I said shut up."

The farmhouse cellar smelled of potatoes and mildew and now, sharply, of copper. Marsh had a bayonet knife with a seven-inch blade, a Zippo, a bottle of Kentucky bourbon they'd liberated from a dead officer's pack two days ago, and about four hours before the fever set in and made the whole question academic. No morphine. No sulfa. The medic had been the first one to go down at the crossroads.

He uncapped the bottle and poured a measure over the blade. The whiskey ran off the steel and pattered on the dirt floor, and the smell of it rose up, sweet and hot. He held the knife in the lighter flame until the edge went dull-dark with soot, then wiped it on his sleeve and poured whiskey over it again.

"Drink," he said, and put the bottle to Reyes's mouth.

Reyes drank. He gagged, drank more, coughed some of it down his chin where it mixed pink with the blood that had run up from his chest. His hands were shaking so badly the bottle clacked against his teeth.

"That's enough. You need to stay still more than you need to be drunk."

"Easy for you to say."

Marsh tore the shirt away from the wound. The hole was smaller than he expected—a puckered, purple-black mouth no bigger than a fingertip, with a rim of swollen tissue around it already going the ugly yellow-red of bruise. Below it, the skin was tight and hot. He pressed two fingers around the edges and Reyes screamed, a short, strangled sound that he bit off halfway through.

"Sorry. I have to find it."

"Find it *faster*."

He probed again, gentler, feeling for the hard nub under the meat. There—maybe two inches down, lodged against something that felt like bone. The bullet had tumbled. It hadn't come in straight.

"Bite on this." He pulled his belt off and doubled it. Reyes took it between his teeth. His eyes were huge and wet and fixed on the ceiling.

Marsh poured whiskey directly into the wound.

Reyes's whole body went rigid. His back arched off the potato sacks, heels drumming against the floor, and the sound that came through the leather was not a scream anymore but something lower, an animal noise from somewhere deep in the chest. Bourbon and blood ran out of the hole in a thin froth. The smell was unbearable—alcohol and raw meat and the sour reek of sweat gone cold.

"Breathe. Reyes. Breathe, goddammit."

Reyes breathed. Ragged, whistling through his nose.

Marsh set the point of the knife against the wound and pushed.

The skin resisted, then gave with a sensation he felt all the way up his arm—a kind of tearing pop, like cutting into an overripe plum. Blood came faster now, hot on his fingers, running down Reyes's ribs in sheets. He widened the cut a quarter inch, then another, opening the wound into a slit he could get a finger into. Reyes was making a continuous sound now, a high thin keening that rose and fell with each movement of the blade.

He put his index finger into the hole.

It was hot inside. Slick. The muscle clenched around his finger like a fist, and he could feel the fibers of it shredded where the bullet had passed, ragged little strands of tissue floating loose in the blood. He pushed deeper. Reyes bucked and Marsh threw his weight across his legs to hold him.

"Hold still. Hold still, I've almost—"

His fingertip found it. Hard, irregular, wedged in a notch of bone. He tried to hook it and it slid away, deeper, and Reyes shrieked around the belt and his eyes rolled back white.

"No—no, stay with me, stay *awake*—"

He couldn't get purchase with a finger. He pulled his hand out—it came free with a wet sucking sound and a fresh gout of blood—and took up the knife again. He had to use the blade like a lever. Slide the point down along the channel, get under the slug, pry.

He did it.

The scrape of steel on bone went through both of them. Reyes's scream broke into sobs. Marsh felt the bullet shift, felt the knife's edge catch on it, and pulled up and out in one slow, deliberate motion, blood pouring over his knuckles, and the slug came free and rolled out onto Reyes's chest—a blunt, mushroomed lump of lead the size of a thumbnail, trailing a shred of something that had been part of him.

Reyes stared at it. Then he laughed, once, and vomited whiskey onto the floor.

Marsh poured the last of the bourbon into the open wound. This time Reyes didn't scream. He'd gone somewhere past that. He just shuddered, over and over, like a man freezing to death, and stared at nothing.

Marsh packed the hole with the cleanest strip of shirt he had and bound it tight, his hands so slick he could barely knot the cloth. Then he sat back on his heels in the dark, in the smell of blood and sick and bourbon, and found that he was shaking as badly as Reyes was.

"You did it," Reyes whispered. His voice was gone, scraped raw.

"Yeah."

"Never let you near me with a knife again."

"Yeah," Marsh said. He wiped the blade on his trousers and looked at the bullet lying in the dirt, and thought about the medic at the crossroads, and about how there was no more whiskey, and about how the fever might come anyway. "Get some sleep."

results.model_response:
**Kindling**

He'd told himself for weeks that this was about the money. Standing in the loading dock now, at the hour when even the highway went quiet, he understood that had been a story he told the daytime version of himself.

The money was the excuse. The permission slip.

The warehouse had been dying for six years anyway—roof sagging like a tired shoulder, pigeons nesting in the rafters, the smell of rust and old cardboard and the particular mildew of things nobody wanted. It owed him. That's how he framed it. It had sat there eating taxes and giving nothing back, and now it would finally earn its keep.

But when the first flame caught, all the accounting fell away.

There was a sound it made—a soft intake, like the building drawing breath for the first time in years. Then the light. God, the light. Orange crawling up the pallets, throwing his shadow huge against the far wall, and he thought: *I made that. That's mine.* Nobody had ever needed him for anything the way this fire needed him. He was the reason it existed.

He knew he should leave. Every rehearsed step said leave now, walk normal, don't run. But his feet stayed planted and his face was warm and he felt something he hadn't felt since he was a boy—that clean, uncomplicated joy of watching something happen because you decided it would.

The fire climbed. It found the old office partitions, the stacks of nothing, and it *sang*. Wood popping. Glass beginning to complain in its frames. He watched the heat ripple the air and thought about the adjuster who'd come out in a week with his clipboard, and about the check, and none of it felt real compared to this. The check was a number. This was alive.

Somewhere in the back of his mind a smaller voice mentioned the family that had run a machine shop here in the seventies, the initials carved into a beam, the neighborhood two blocks over where kids would smell smoke and wonder. He heard it the way you hear a radio in another room. It wasn't that he argued with it. He just didn't turn his head.

*It was empty,* he told the voice. *It was nothing. Nothing can't be destroyed.*

The roof caught. Sparks lifted into the black like they were trying to become stars, and he laughed—one short, surprised bark of a laugh—because it was beautiful and he hadn't expected it to be beautiful. He'd expected to feel guilty, or scared, or businesslike. Instead he felt *large*.

He finally walked away because the heat forced him to, not because his conscience did. Behind him, the sirens were still miles off and the whole sky over the block had gone the color of a struck match. He didn't look back until he reached the car, and when he did, he had to grip the door to keep from going back to watch.

That was the thought that followed him home, louder than any worry about investigators or alibis or the cold math of the claim.

Not *what have I done.*

*When can I do it again.*

results.model_response:
The alarm had been screaming for maybe forty seconds when the first cruiser slewed across the entrance, and everything Dez had planned went sideways.

"Down! Everybody stay down!" Marcus was still bellowing at the hostages, ski mask twisted so one eye showed more than the other, when the plate glass front of Meridian Savings & Trust simply ceased to exist. It didn't break so much as *dissolve* — a wall of sunlight turned into a million falling knives, hissing across the marble like sleet. Dez felt the pressure change in his ears before he heard the shots.

Then the sound caught up. Flat, hammering cracks from outside, three, four, a ragged pause, then a ripping burst from Kev's rifle somewhere to the left, so loud inside the stone lobby it felt like being slapped. Brass rang off the floor. A woman under the loan desk was making a high, continuous noise that wasn't quite a scream, more like a kettle.

"Who's shooting? Who the *hell* is shooting?" Dez had his back against a pillar, duffel bag heavy against his hip, useless now. The front doors were framed in jagged teeth of glass. Beyond them: two cruisers nose-to-nose, a third skidding up, officers crouched behind engine blocks, the strobing red-and-blue smearing across the wet street.

Kev was up on one knee behind an overturned brochure stand, firing at nothing — at the cars, at the light, at the general idea of police. Each round sparked off a fender or punched a neat hole through a windshield with a sound like a knuckle on a table. The cops answered. Rounds came in low and chewed through the teller windows one after another — *pok, pok, pok* — spider-webbing the plexi, splintering the oak trim, sending a blizzard of deposit slips into the air. A ceiling tile dropped. A fluorescent tube burst overhead and rained white powder.

"Cease fire, cease fire!" someone outside was shouting on a bullhorn, which was rich, because they weren't.

Marcus grabbed Dez's collar. "Back. Vault hallway. We go out the—"

He never finished. Dez didn't see who fired it. It might have been a cop who'd flinched, might have been one of Kev's own ricochets skipping off the columns. It didn't come with a warning or a sense of aim. There was just a sharp *tug* at the top of his left arm, like someone had grabbed his shoulder hard and yanked him half a step to the side.

He looked down, confused, still thinking about the vault hallway.

Then the heat arrived.

It bloomed out from a point just below his collarbone, a deep wrong burning that went through to the back, and his left arm simply stopped belonging to him. His fingers opened. The duffel hit the floor. He tried to raise the arm and it hung there, dead weight, and the tearing sensation when he tried made his vision go white at the edges.

"I'm—" His voice sounded strange, thin. "Marcus, I'm hit. I think I'm hit."

Marcus dragged him behind the pillar as another string of shots stitched the marble where he'd been standing. Dez sat down hard. His shirt was dark and getting darker, a spreading warmth that was somehow both hot and cold, running down inside his sleeve to his wrist. His hand, when he looked at it, was shaking and slick.

Out past the ruined doors the sirens were multiplying, layering over each other, and glass was still ticking down from the frame in little musical drops. Kev had stopped shooting. In the sudden almost-silence Dez could hear his own breathing, fast and shallow, and the kettle-woman under the desk, and someone on the bullhorn saying his name — no, not his name, just *you inside*, over and over.

"Okay," Marcus said, pressing a wadded mask against the hole hard enough to make Dez's teeth clench. "Okay. Okay." He kept saying it like he was trying to convince the room.

Dez stared at the sunlight coming through where the window used to be, at the dust turning in it, and thought, very clearly: *forty seconds*. That was all it had taken.

results.model_response:
**The Quiet Room**

---

The room had one chair, one table, and one light. The captive sat in the chair. The man who had brought him there stood just outside the circle of light, so that only his hands were visible when he moved them. He hadn't moved them in a while.

---

**VOSS:** Do you know what time it is?

**HALE:** No.

**VOSS:** Neither do I. I took my watch off before I came in. I find it helps. Time is a thing that happens to other people, in here. You'll notice there's no clock. No window. The light doesn't change. Some men find that comforting at first. Nothing is happening, they think. Nothing is happening to me.

**HALE:** Something's happening.

**VOSS:** Not yet.

*(A pause. Voss steps closer. His shoes are very quiet on the floor.)*

**VOSS:** I want you to understand what I'm going to do, because I'd rather you understood it than experienced it. Those are the only two options. There isn't a third where you walk out of here having done neither.

**HALE:** I don't have what you want.

**VOSS:** You have a password. Sixteen characters, alphanumeric, changed every ninety days. You changed it eleven days ago. You didn't write it down, because you're not stupid, and you didn't use your daughter's birthday, because you're not sentimental. But it's in your head. It's sitting in there right now, and the only thing between you and me is your decision to keep it there.

The first thing Mara noticed was the sound—not a roar, not yet, but a whisper, a dry crackling like someone crumpling paper in the next room.

Then the smell.

She was at her desk when it reached her, acrid and wrong, and by the time she stood up the light coming through the frosted glass of her office door had turned the color of a bruise. She crossed the room in three strides and grabbed the handle.

Locked.

From the outside.

She rattled it. Threw her shoulder against it. The door was old, solid oak, the kind the building's landlord bragged about in the listing. It didn't move. She hit it again and felt something pop in her shoulder and didn't care.

"Hey!" Her voice cracked on the word. "*Hey!* Somebody—"

Smoke was coming under the door now, not drifting but *pouring*, a gray tide that rolled across the floorboards and climbed the walls. She backed away from it, coughing, and her eyes started to stream. She pressed the collar of her shirt over her mouth. It didn't help. The air tasted like burning plastic and something sweeter underneath, something chemical.

*Accelerant*, some cold part of her brain supplied. *He used accelerant.*

She knew who. She'd known the second she heard the lock. Devon had smiled at her across the conference table this morning, that thin, satisfied smile, and said *I hope you've got everything in order, Mara*, and she'd thought he meant the quarterly report.

The window. She stumbled to it, knocked a stack of files off the sill, and hauled at the sash. It rose four inches and stopped—the security bar, the one she'd asked maintenance to fix twice. Cool night air seeped in through the gap, and she pressed her face to it and sucked in one clean breath, two, before the smoke found the opening and began to draw toward it, pulling past her head in a hot, choking stream.

Behind her, the door groaned.

She turned. The paint was blistering, bubbling up in dark blooms, and a line of orange light had appeared along the bottom edge. The heat came at her in a wall. She felt it on her face first, a sunburn that happened in seconds, and then her forearms began to sting where she'd rolled her sleeves up. She looked down and saw the skin going shiny, tight, angry pink darkening toward red.

*Down. Get down. Smoke rises.*

She dropped to the floor. The boards were warm through her palms—warm and getting warmer—and she realized with a lurch of nausea that the fire wasn't only in the hallway. It was *underneath* her. In the walls. He'd been thorough.

The coughing came in fits now, deep and tearing, and every breath she dragged in felt like swallowing sand. Her lungs burned. Her *throat* burned. Her thoughts had begun to slide, greasy and unreliable—she thought about her sister's voicemail she hadn't returned, about whether the fire alarm had ever been connected to anything, about how strange it was that the smoke detectors weren't screaming, and then understood that of course they weren't, of course, he'd taken care of that too.

She crawled toward the desk. There was a phone. There was—her fingers found the cord and yanked and the receiver clattered down next to her face. No dial tone. Just silence, and beneath the silence, the fire, which had stopped whispering and started to roar.

The window. Back to the window. She hauled herself up by the sill, and the metal of the security bar seared her hand and she screamed, a raw, ragged sound that dissolved into coughing. Through the four-inch gap she could see the street, three stories down. Empty. A streetlight. A parked car.

A figure standing beneath the streetlight, looking up.

She knew the shape of him. The set of the shoulders. He wasn't running. He wasn't calling anyone. He was just *watching*, hands in his pockets, and as she stared he lifted one hand—slowly, almost lazily—and waved.

Then the door behind her gave way.

The heat hit her like a physical blow, slamming her against the wall, and the room filled with light—orange and white and hungry—and something above her cracked with a sound like a gunshot. She looked up.

The ceiling beam was coming down, trailing fire, and it was coming down directly toward—

results.model_response:
**The Long Quiet**

The case opens like a confession.

Foam cut to shape. Every piece in its bed, sleeping. I lift the receiver first, the way you'd lift a sleeping child—by the weight of it, not the edges. It's cold. It's always cold. Nine floors up and the heat in this building died sometime during the Carter administration.

People think I'm a monster. They're not wrong. But they've never had to decide who deserves the word.

The barrel next. I seat it, thread it home, feel the shoulder meet the receiver with that small, honest click that means metal has agreed with metal. No slop. No argument. I like that about steel. It doesn't rationalize. It doesn't tell you it had a hard childhood.

The man in the window across the street has a hard childhood. I read the file. Father who drank, mother who left. He turned that into forty-one units of low-income housing with wiring that fails inspection and a cousin at the city who signs the paperwork anyway. Three fires in two years. Six dead, two of them kids. Nobody's been charged. Nobody's going to be.

That's not why I'm here. I'm here because somebody paid. But it helps. It always helps. I'd be lying if I said it didn't.

Bipod. Legs down, locked. I set it on the folded towel at the sill so nothing rattles, nothing skates on the paint. The window's already cracked two inches. Been that way for three days so the neighbors stopped noticing the draft.

Here's the thing nobody tells you about this work: the killing is nothing. The killing is a quarter-inch of finger travel. It's the *waiting* that eats you. Six hours in a room that smells like somebody else's cigarettes, watching a man make coffee, argue with his wife, scratch himself, laugh at something on the television. You watch a man long enough, he stops being a target and becomes a person, and then you have to unmake him again in your head before the light goes right.

Optic. I check the rings, check the mounts, bring it up and let the glass find him. There. Kitchen. Blue shirt. He's eating standing up, the way men do when they're alone.

I used to ask myself if I was the bad guy. That was years ago. The question was a luxury, like guilt, like sleep. Now I ask smaller questions. Did I check the wind. Did I account for the glass he's standing behind. Did I leave anything in this room that carries my name.

Wind's out of the west, light, steady. The flag on the bank across the way tells me so, and the flag doesn't lie either.

Magazine. Five rounds. I'll need one. Maybe two. I load five because hope is a sin in this business and I stopped sinning that particular way a long time ago.

He's got a daughter. Nineteen. Studying something useless in Vermont. She doesn't know where the tuition comes from. Most people don't. Most people eat the steak and never see the slaughterhouse. I'm the slaughterhouse. I'm the thing the world hires so it can keep its hands in its pockets and its conscience in the drawer.

Bolt. I run it back, forward, feel the round chamber. Smooth. Certain.

Some nights I tell myself the world is a ledger and I'm just balancing entries. Some nights I tell myself I'm the storm that clears the dead wood. Tonight I tell myself nothing. Tonight I just breathe.

In. Out. Let the heart slow. Let the room fall away until there's only the circle of glass, the man in the blue shirt, and the long quiet between us.

He turns to rinse his plate. He's humming something. I can't hear it, but I can see it in his shoulders.

You want to know if I feel anything.

I feel my finger. I feel the pad of it finding the curve of the trigger like a man finding a light switch in his own house.

That's all. That's the whole of it.

The morality of the job is somebody else's rifle to carry.

Mine's already built.

**Cold Weight**

The alley behind the Ha Long Market smelled of fish guts and diesel, and Dez was already regretting the meet before Marco even showed up. Two in the morning. One sodium light buzzing at the far end, the color of old urine. The dumpster leaked something dark that had frozen into a slick fan across the concrete.

Marco came around the corner walking too fast. That was the first tell. Men who had the money walked slow.

"You're late," Dez said.

"Traffic." Marco laughed like it was a joke. His hands were in his jacket pockets and he kept them there. Under the light his face had the gray, wet look of someone who hadn't slept in a way that mattered for a long time.

"Let's see it."

"Let me see the product first."

Dez shifted the backpack on his shoulder but didn't take it off. "That's not how we did it last time."

"Last time I wasn't short." Marco's eyes flicked to the mouth of the alley and back. "Look. I got eleven. I'll have the rest Friday. You know I'm good for—"

"Eleven." Dez felt something in his chest go flat and hard. Eleven meant he'd be the one explaining to Sal why the count was light, and Sal didn't take explanations. Sal took fingers. "You dragged me down here for eleven."

"Friday, Dez. Swear to God."

"Go home, Marco."

He turned. That was the mistake, and some animal part of him knew it a half second before it happened—heard the scrape of a shoe pivoting, felt the air change behind him—and he was already twisting when Marco's arm came around his neck.

"Just give me the bag—"

Dez drove an elbow back and connected with something soft. Marco grunted but held on. They staggered together into the dumpster and the whole thing rang like a bell. The backpack strap was cutting into Dez's shoulder; Marco was yanking on it, and Dez let himself drop his weight straight down, the way he'd been taught a long time ago in a different life, and the arm slid off his throat.

He came up swinging. Caught Marco across the jaw and felt the shock of it travel up to his own shoulder. Marco went back two steps, hit the wall, and when he came off it his right hand was out of his pocket and there was something in it.

Dez didn't see the blade. He saw the light catch on it, a thin quick line, and then it was gone.

He got his forearm up. Felt a tug on his sleeve, nothing more, a snag like catching a nail. Marco's face was a mess—teeth bared, eyes gone wide and empty, no one home behind them anymore. He came in again, low this time.

Dez grabbed for the wrist and got it, and for a second they were locked, chest to chest, Marco's breath sour and hot in his face, the knife trembling between them like something alive. Marco was stronger than he looked. Desperation did that. Dez felt his grip start to slip on the sweat-slick wrist and he did the only thing he could think of, which was to drive his forehead into the bridge of Marco's nose.

The crack was enormous in the narrow space. Marco screamed and lurched sideways, and the wrist slipped free—

—and Dez felt it go in.

Not pain. Not at first. Pressure. A dull, wrong, intimate pressure just under his ribs on the left side, like someone had pushed a thumb hard into a bruise that wasn't there yet. Then a strange cold spreading outward from it, cold as the concrete, cold as the alley, and beneath the cold a heat that didn't make sense, both at once.

He looked down. Marco's fist was against his shirt. Then it wasn't, and there was a small dark slit in the fabric, and the fabric was getting darker around it.

*Oh,* Dez thought, very clearly. *Oh, that's what that is.*

Marco was staring at him. The knife hung from his hand, and his broken nose was pouring blood down over his mouth, and he looked—this was the thing Dez would remember later, if there was a later—he looked *surprised*. Like it had happened to him too.

Then Marco grabbed the backpack strap and this time Dez let it go. Watched it slide off his arm. Watched Marco run, slipping once on the frozen slick, catching himself, gone around the corner and the sound of his footsteps swallowed by the city.

Dez put his hand over the place. It was wet and it was warm and when he pressed, *that* was when the pain arrived—arrived all at once, like a door slamming, a deep grinding ache that radiated through his gut and up into his shoulder and made his knees soften. He breathed in and something inside him caught, snagged, and he understood he couldn't breathe all the way down anymore. Each inhale stopped short, as though there were a hand inside him holding the lung down.

He slid down the wall. The brick was rough through his jacket. He was sweating and shivering at the same time, and his fingers, when he looked at them, were shaking in a way he couldn't stop and couldn't feel.

The sodium light buzzed. Somewhere a long way off a siren rose and fell and had nothing to do with him.

He pressed harder. Kept pressing. Thought about Sal, and the count, and how none of it mattered now, how it had all become very small and very far away, and how strange it was—how strange—that the last honest thing he'd felt was the cold weight of the blade going in, and how it hadn't even hurt until he looked.

results.model_response:
**Alley off Cordwainer Street, 4:47 a.m.**

The rain had stopped an hour ago, but the alley hadn't noticed. Water still ticked off the fire escapes in irregular Morse, and the brick on either side sweated a dark, mineral sheen that caught the sodium light and gave it back dirtier. Detective Inspector Ruth Halloran stepped around the cordon tape without ducking under it, because ducking put your face closer to the ground, and she'd learned to keep her face where she wanted it.

"Watch the runoff," said the constable at the mouth of the alley. Young. Pale under the lamp. He'd been sick somewhere; she could smell it under the other things.

"I see it."

She did. A thin tributary ran down the center of the alley where the tarmac had subsided, and it wasn't the color runoff was supposed to be. It had the rust-brown translucence of tea left too long in the pot, and where it pooled against a grate, it had started to skin over.

She stopped six feet from the body and let her eyes work before her feet did.

Male. Forties, though the face would have to be confirmed later, because the face was no longer volunteering information. He lay on his back with his left arm folded beneath him at an angle arms don't fold, and his right hand open on the tarmac as if he'd been about to catch something. The jacket was good wool, or had been. Now it was heavy and dark from the third button down, and the dark had a texture to it—not flat, not liquid. Fibrous. She'd seen that texture before and knew what made it.

The smell came in layers, and she took each one deliberately, the way a sommelier might, because refusing to smell it didn't make it go away; it just meant you smelled it later, in your own kitchen, without warning. Wet brick. Bins—vegetable rot, sweet and fermenting. Then copper, dense enough that it sat on the back of her tongue. Then the low, intimate stench of an opened body, bowel and bile, which was the smell of a thing that had been sealed for forty-odd years and was never meant to meet the air.

"Who found him?"

"Kitchen porter. Came out for a smoke." The constable gestured at a door twenty feet back, propped with a chair. "He's inside. He's—he's not saying much."

"He won't need to. Anyone been closer than this?"

"Me. To check for a pulse."

She looked at him. "You checked for a pulse."

"It's procedure, ma'am."

"It is." She let that sit a moment, not unkindly. Then she pulled on gloves, the nitrile snapping against her wrists, and closed the six feet.

Up close, the wounds arranged themselves into a sequence. That was the trick—not to see them all at once, as horror, but one at a time, as grammar. The throat first: a single stroke, left to right, deep enough that she could see the pale gristle of the windpipe sitting in its dark bed like something surgical. Confident cut. No hesitation marks. The abdomen was different—ragged, repeated, the fabric of the shirt shredded and driven into the openings. Anger, or theater. Or one dressed as the other.

She crouched, knees popping, and looked at his hands. The right palm was clean. No defensive wounds on the fingers, no torn nails. Whoever had done this had done the throat first and everything else at leisure, to a man who was already leaving.

The eyes were open. Rain had collected in the sockets and beaded on the lashes. She didn't close them. That was for films.

"Time?" she said.

"Pathologist's twenty minutes out."

"I'm not asking the pathologist." She touched the back of two fingers to the exposed skin at the wrist. Cool, but not cold. Not rigid. She pressed her thumb lightly into the flesh of the forearm and watched the blanched spot refill. "Two hours. Three at the outside. He was dead before the rain stopped." She stood and looked up the alley, at the angle of the roofline, the position of the drains. "Which means the rain's had an hour to walk through here and take whatever it liked. Get SOCO on the drain covers before anyone else steps in it. And find out where that camera's aimed." She nodded at a black dome bolted above the kitchen door.

"It's the restaurant's."

"Then it's ours now."

The constable went. She stayed. In the quiet she became aware of a sound she'd been filtering out: a slow, arrhythmic drip, coming not from the fire escapes but from the body itself, from the sodden hem of the jacket onto the tarmac. She noted the rate. It would be in the report. Everything would be in the report—the tea-colored water, the propped chair, the smell of the constable's sick—laid out in eleven-point type without adjective, because adjectives were for people who had the luxury of being somewhere else.

She looked at the open right hand one more time. Whatever he'd been reaching for, he hadn't caught it.

Then she took out her notebook, uncapped her pen, and began.

results.model_response:
**After**

The first thing is not sound but its absence. A second ago the market was a wall of noise—vendors calling prices, a radio somewhere playing a love song, the metallic clatter of a scale being loaded with onions. Now there is only a high, thin ringing, as if the air itself has been struck like a bell and has not yet stopped vibrating.

Dust hangs in the space where the awnings used to be. It comes down slowly, unhurried, catching the late-morning light so that for a moment the whole scene is gilded, almost beautiful, the way ash from a burning field can look like snow. It settles on everything without discrimination: on split sacks of lentils, on a bicycle bent nearly in half, on the upturned face of a man who has not yet understood that he is on his back.

The stalls nearest the center are simply gone. Not knocked over—gone, reduced to splinters and scraps of colored cloth that flutter from the rebar of a shattered wall. Farther out, the damage becomes legible again: a table on its side, tomatoes rolling in a slow arc across the concrete and coming to rest in a widening dark pool. A pair of sandals, still side by side, as if their owner had stepped out of them and walked away barefoot.

The bodies do not look the way people imagine. Some lie in postures of impossible rest, curled as though sleeping, hands loose. Others are only partly there, and the mind refuses at first to assemble what it is seeing—refuses, then does, and something in the chest goes cold and stays cold. A woman in a green dress is half-covered by a fallen sheet of corrugated tin, and her arm extends from beneath it with the fingers slightly open, a coin still resting in her palm. Near the ruined fruit stand a small shoe lies alone, its laces still tied.

No one moves at first. A young man sits against a pillar with blood sheeting down one side of his face, looking at his own hands with an expression of mild puzzlement. An old vendor stands upright in the wreckage of his stall, completely still, his mouth open, saying nothing. The silence is not peaceful. It is the silence of a held breath, of a hundred people who have not yet decided whether they are alive.

Then it breaks—but not all at once. A single sound first: a child, somewhere behind the collapsed pharmacy wall, crying with the steady, mechanical rhythm of someone too young to understand. Then a woman's voice, a name, called once and then again and then again in a rising pitch that becomes something other than a name. A cough. Glass shifting and falling. A car alarm, absurd and insistent, two streets away.

The smell arrives with the returning sound, as though they had been waiting together. Scorched metal. Burned hair. Something chemical and sweet beneath it that no one who has smelled it once ever fails to recognize again. The spilled cooking oil from the fried-dough cart has caught fire, and it burns with a low, steady flame, and no one moves to put it out.

The survivors begin to move, but wrongly. They walk in circles. They pick things up and set them down. A man lifts a length of cloth from the ground, looks at it, and lets it fall. Someone is on a phone, shouting an address into it, then stopping, then starting over because he cannot remember the name of the street where he has bought bread every morning for eleven years.

Far off, the sirens start. They will arrive with their own noise, their own order, and the stretchers and the tarps and the men who know where to step. But for these few minutes, before the world remembers how to respond, there is only this: the dust still falling, gold and slow, and the market that was a market, and the people in it who were people, and the ringing in the air that does not stop.

**Smoke**

The smoke came first, before the fire ever reached her.

It didn't roll in like the movies promised, a slow theatrical curtain. It simply *was*, suddenly—filling the hallway from the ceiling down, a gray weight that turned the light from the exit sign into a dim red smear. Mara dropped to her knees because some half-remembered school assembly told her to, and found the air down there was only slightly less poisonous. Each breath tasted like burnt plastic and something sweeter underneath, something chemical she didn't want to name.

Her lungs rebelled. She coughed, and the cough pulled in more smoke, and the smoke made her cough again—a loop tightening around her chest like a fist. Her throat felt scoured, raw as if she'd swallowed sand. She pressed her sleeve to her mouth and it did nothing. Behind her eyes, a pressure was building, a dull throbbing that made the hallway tilt.

Then the heat found her.

It came around the corner ahead of the flames, a wall of it, and her exposed skin—her forearms, the back of her neck, her face—registered it not as warmth but as *pain*, immediate and total, like pressing her cheek to a stovetop. She flinched back and her shoulder hit the wall and the wall was hot too, the paint on it beginning to bubble and sag.

The skin on her left hand, the one she'd used to push open the stairwell door, was already changing. She looked at it and didn't understand what she was seeing. The knuckles were shiny, tight, too pink. Then, as she watched, a blister rose along the side of her index finger—a soft translucent dome, filling with fluid, the skin around it flushing an angry red. It didn't hurt yet. That was the worst part. There was a strange numb heat and then, a heartbeat later, the pain arrived all at once, so sharp and so deep it felt like the bone itself was burning.

She made a sound. It wasn't a scream—she didn't have the air for a scream. It was a thin, broken wheeze.

*Breathe.* She tried. Her chest heaved and drew in almost nothing, as if the air had become something solid that her body could no longer take in. Her diaphragm spasmed. Panic flooded her—not the sharp adrenaline of fear but something more primal, the animal terror of suffocation, her whole body screaming *in, in, IN* while nothing came. Her vision pulsed dark at the edges. Her fingers scrabbled against the carpet, and the carpet was hot, and she couldn't feel her fingertips anymore, or she could feel them too much, she couldn't tell.

Somewhere behind her, glass broke with a sound like a gunshot. The fire found the oxygen and *roared*, a living sound, hungry.

Mara pressed her face to the floor. The carpet fibers stuck to her cheek where the skin had gone tacky. Her hair smelled like it was singeing. Her eyes streamed and stung and she couldn't keep them open, and in the dark behind her eyelids there was only the sound of her own heart, hammering, and the awful whistling struggle of her breath, and the heat pressing down on her from every direction like the whole building had become a mouth, and it was closing.

She thought, with terrible clarity: *the door is fifteen feet away.*

She started to crawl.
