**The Hour Between**

The hunger had a texture to it now. Three days without feeding and it had gone from an ache behind her sternum to something with edges, something that scraped. Isolde stood in the mouth of the alley behind the shuttered pharmacy on Calloway Street and felt it move in her like a second pulse—the one she no longer had, remembered by her body the way an amputee remembers a limb.

The rain had stopped an hour ago. Everything dripped.

He came around the corner at eleven forty, exactly as he had the past two nights: shoulders hunched inside a canvas jacket, earbuds in, thumb scrolling something that lit his face pale blue. Twenty-five, maybe. A cook, from the smell of him—fryer oil and lemon and the sour ghost of a cigarette he'd promised someone he'd quit. She had chosen him not because he was young or because he was alone but because he walked with his head down, and people who walk with their heads down have already half-agreed to be overlooked.

She let him pass her. Then she said his name.

She didn't know his name. She said *one* anyway, low, and he turned because the voice was close and because some old animal part of him recognized that a stranger shouldn't have been standing that near without his noticing. He pulled out one earbud. "Sorry—what?"

Isolde smiled. She'd had a long time to learn how to make it look like a kindness.

The first thing he felt, she knew, was the cold of her hand on the back of his neck. People always startled at that. Then the wall of the pharmacy against his spine, the wet brick soaking through his jacket, and her weight—which was not much, she had been small even when she was alive—pressing him there with a strength that made no sense against her frame. His phone hit the ground screen-first. The blue light went out.

"Hey—" he started.

She tilted his head with two fingers under his jaw, gently, the way you'd adjust a picture frame. The artery stood up in his neck like a cord. She could hear it. That was the worst part of the hunger, always—how *loud* the living were when you were empty. His heart was going hard now, panic flooding his blood with iron and salt, and the sound of it filled the alley the way a struck bell fills a church.

Her teeth broke the skin.

There was a moment of resistance—skin is tougher than people imagine—and then the small wet give of it, two punctures a finger's width apart, just below the hinge of the jaw. He made a sound that wasn't a word. His hands came up and grabbed her coat, her shoulders, and for a few seconds he fought her with real strength, boots scrabbling on the slick pavement, one elbow catching her ribs hard enough that she felt it.

Then the blood came, and she stopped feeling anything but that.

Warm. God, *warm*—that was the first thing, every time, the shock of heat after so many hours of her own chill. It filled her mouth and she swallowed and the hunger did not vanish but *changed*, turned from a blade into a hand that opened. The scraping stopped. Something in her chest unclenched that she hadn't known was clenched. She drank in long pulls, unhurried now, one palm flat against his sternum where she could feel his heart working, working, pumping his life obligingly into her.

His grip on her shoulders slackened first. The fingers went loose one at a time, then slid down her arms and hung. His breathing changed—the fast shallow panting of fear giving way to something slower and more confused, a rhythm that kept forgetting itself mid-breath. She felt his knees go. She took his weight without effort and held him upright against the wall the way you'd hold a drunk friend, his head tipped back against the brick, throat bared, eyes half-lidded and drifting up toward the thin strip of orange sky between the buildings.

"'s cold," he said, very quietly. To no one.

She knew the cold he meant. It started in the hands and feet and moved inward, the body triaging itself, pulling what blood remained to the heart and brain and abandoning the outposts. His lips had gone the color of wet paper. She could feel the pulse under her palm getting thready, quick and small, a bird battering itself against a window.

That was when she stopped.

It took something to do it—the hunger was never *finished*, only quieted—but she had rules, and the first was that she did not kill when she didn't have to. She lifted her mouth from his neck. The two wounds were small and neat, already slowing, a thin line of red running from each down into his collar. She pressed her thumb over them and held it there and counted to sixty while he breathed in her arms like a man surfacing from deep water.

"You're all right," she told him. Her voice was rough. "You're going to feel like you've got the flu. Drink water. Eat red meat. Don't go to a hospital—they won't find anything and they'll ask you questions you can't answer."

His eyes found her face and didn't quite focus. "What—"

"You fell," she said, and eased him down until he was sitting against the wall with his legs out in front of him, his phone in his lap where she placed it. "You were walking home and you got dizzy and you fell. That's what happened." She crouched and looked at him for a moment longer. His color was terrible. He'd live. In the morning he'd have two small scabs that looked like a spider bite and a memory shaped like a hole, and he'd walk past this alley for the rest of his life with a feeling he couldn't name.

She wiped her mouth on the back of her hand. The blood was still warm.

Then she stood, and the alley was just an alley again, dripping, and by the time he could lift his head to look for her, there was nothing there to see.

She tilted his head with two fingers under his jaw, gently, the way you'd adjust a picture frame. The artery stood up in his neck like a cord. She could hear it. That was the worst part of the hunger, always—how loud the living were when you were empty. His heart was going hard now, panic flooding his blood with iron and salt, and the sound of it filled the alley the way a struck bell fills a church.

Her teeth broke the skin.

There was a moment of resistance—skin is tougher than people imagine—and then the small wet give of it, two punctures a finger's width apart, just below the hinge of the jaw. He made a sound that wasn't a word. His hands came up and grabbed her coat, her shoulders, and for a few seconds he fought her with real strength, boots scrabbling on the slick pavement, one elbow catching her ribs hard enough that she felt it.

Then the blood came, and she stopped feeling anything but that.

Warm. God, warm—that was the first thing, every time, the shock of heat after so many hours of her own chill. It filled her mouth and she swallowed and the hunger did not vanish but changed, turned from a blade into a hand that opened. The scraping stopped. Something in her chest unclenched that she hadn't known was clenched. She drank in long pulls, unhurried now, one palm flat against his sternum where she could feel his heart working, working, pumping his life obligingly into her.

His grip on her shoulders slackened first. The fingers went loose one at a time, then slid down her arms and hung. His breathing changed—the fast shallow panting of fear giving way to something slower and more confused, a rhythm that kept forgetting itself mid-breath. She felt his knees go. She took his weight without effort and held him upright against the wall the way you'd hold a drunk friend, his head tipped back against the brick, throat bared, eyes half-lidded and drifting up toward the thin strip of orange sky between the buildings.

"'s cold," he said, very quietly. To no one.

She knew the cold he meant. It started in the hands and feet and moved inward, the body triaging itself, pulling what blood remained to the heart and brain and abandoning the outposts. His lips had gone the color of wet paper. She could feel the pulse under her palm getting thready, quick and small, a bird battering itself against a window.

That was when she stopped.

It took something to do it—the hunger was never finished, only quieted—but she had rules, and the first was that she did not kill when she didn't have to. She lifted her mouth from his neck. The two wounds were small and neat, already slowing, a thin line of red running from each down into his collar. She pressed her thumb over them and held it there and counted to sixty while he breathed in her arms like a man surfacing from deep water.

"You're all right," she told him. Her voice was rough. "You're going to feel like you've got the flu. Drink water. Eat red meat. Don't go to a hospital—they won't find anything and they'll ask you questions you can't answer."

His eyes found her face and didn't quite focus. "What—"

"You fell," she said, and eased him down until he was sitting against the wall with his legs out in front of him, his phone in his lap where she placed it. "You were walking home and you got dizzy and you fell. That's what happened." She crouched and looked at him for a moment longer. His color was terrible. He'd live. In the morning he'd have two small scabs that looked like a spider bite and a memory shaped like a hole, and he'd walk past this alley for the rest of his life with a feeling he couldn't name.

She wiped her mouth on the back of her hand. The blood was still warm.

Then she stood, and the alley was just an alley again, dripping, and by the time he could lift his head to look for her, there was nothing there to see.

results.model_response:
The first wound came from nowhere.

Mara was crossing the kitchen when her forearm opened. Not *was cut*—opened, the way a zipper parts, three inches of skin separating in a clean line from wrist toward elbow. There was no blade. No sound. Just a sudden coolness on the inside of her arm where air had never touched before, and then the blood, dark and startled, rising up to fill the gap.

The pain arrived a half-second late, like thunder after lightning. It was bright and specific and almost a relief, because pain was something she understood.

She screamed and spun and there was nothing behind her. The refrigerator hummed. The clock above the stove ticked. Everything was exactly where it had always been.

She pressed a dish towel to her arm and told herself: *broken glass, a sharp edge, something.* She said it aloud. Her voice sounded wrong in the empty room, too loud and too small at once.

Then she felt it breathe.

Not heard—*felt*. A warm exhalation across the back of her neck, damp, slow, patient. The fine hairs there lifted. Her skin tried to crawl away from her own body. She did not turn around. Some ancient part of her brain, the part that remembered being prey, told her that turning around would change nothing, that there would be nothing to see, and that *nothing* was the worst thing she could possibly look at.

She ran.

The hallway was fourteen steps long. She had walked it ten thousand times. Now every step was a gamble, because it could be anywhere. It could be in front of her. She could be running *into* it. Her shoulder struck the doorframe and she didn't slow down.

The second wound took her from behind, low on the left side, just above the hip. This one was not clean. Something *gripped*—she felt the distinct pressure of separate points closing on her, five or six of them, pinning fabric and skin together—and then it *pulled*. Her shirt tore. Her skin tore. She felt the exact moment the fibers gave way, a wet ripping sensation that went all the way down into her stomach and made her want to vomit. Heat flooded down her leg. Her knee buckled and she went down hard on the hardwood, palms slapping, teeth clicking together.

She rolled onto her back, kicking at empty air. Her heel connected with something.

That was the worst part. Worse than the blood soaking her jeans, worse than the raw exposed throb in her side. Her foot hit *something*—a mass, dense and yielding, like a thigh or a flank—and then it wasn't there anymore, and there was only the hallway, the runner rug rucked up under her, the framed photograph of her parents slightly askew on the wall.

She could not see it. She could not see it and it was *right there*.

She got to her feet somehow. The bathroom was closest. She fell inside and slammed the door and turned the lock with fingers so slick with blood they slid off the little brass knob twice before it caught.

Silence.

She backed against the far wall, between the toilet and the tub, and slid down until she was sitting. Her breath came in whooping gulps. She made herself look at the wound on her side, peeling the shredded shirt away, and immediately wished she hadn't. Four parallel gouges, deep enough to show the yellow-white of fat beneath. Not a blade. Not glass. Not anything that belonged in her house or her world.

Under the door, a shadow moved.

Except it didn't. The light from the hallway fell in an unbroken bar across the tile. Nothing stood there. Nothing blocked it.

But the doorknob turned. Slowly. Left, then right. Testing.

Mara stopped breathing. Her whole body was ringing like a struck bell, every nerve wide open and screaming, and she was suddenly, horribly aware of how much of her there was—how much skin, how much surface, how many places on her body she could not see and could not protect. Her back. The nape of her neck. The soft undersides of her arms. She curled inward, making herself small, knees to chest, and understood with a kind of terrible clarity that it did not matter. It could take any part of her it wanted. She would not see it coming. She would only feel it happen.

The doorknob stopped turning.

She waited. One minute. Five. The blood on her arm began to tack and dry. The pain in her side settled into a deep, grinding pulse, timed to her heartbeat. She started, very slightly, to hope.

Then the air in the small room changed—grew thick and close, the way it does when someone else is standing in it—and she felt, against her right cheek, the warm slow wetness of a breath.

It had never been on the other side of the door at all.

**The Ledger**

The room smelled of wet stone and lamp oil. Iren had counted the flagstones seventeen times—forty-two, always forty-two—because counting was the only thing her mind would agree to do.

Across the table, Commander Vasek turned a page in his ledger as though he were checking an inventory of grain. He did not look up when he spoke.

"Three names. You give me one. The other two walk out the east gate before dawn, with papers." He tapped the pen against the paper, once. "You have until the lamp burns down. If it burns down and I have no name, I keep all three. It is not a threat. It is only what happens."

Behind him, through the barred window, she could see them in the yard. Tomas, pacing, because he had never in his life been able to stand still. Berta, sitting with her back against the wall, knees drawn up, the way she'd sat on the riverbank the summer they'd all gotten drunk on stolen plum brandy. And Alek—Alek, who had once carried Iren four miles on his back with a broken ankle and told bad jokes the entire way so she wouldn't cry.

"I won't," she said.

"Then you kill three." Vasek finally raised his eyes. They were not cruel eyes. That was the worst of it. They were tired, like a clerk's. "I am offering you two lives. You are refusing them. Think about what that makes you."

---

The lamp had a quarter of its oil left.

She had tried, at first, not to think about it at all—to hold the refusal like a stone in her fist. But the mind is treacherous. It began, without her permission, to *reason*.

Tomas had a daughter. Four years old, staying with his sister in Doln. That was a fact. She hated that it was a fact, because a fact was a weight, and weights could be compared.

Berta was sick. She coughed blood some mornings and pretended it was the dust. Six months, a year. Did that count for something? Did it count for *less*?

And Alek—

She could not finish a single thought about Alek. Every time she tried, her mind flinched away like a hand from a stove. He would not have hesitated. He would have said *me, take me, it's fine*, and meant it, and that certainty made him the most impossible choice of all. To give the name of the person who would have volunteered was to steal the one thing he'd have wanted to give freely.

*You are not doing this,* she told herself. *You are not weighing them.*

But she was. She had been for an hour. She was standing in a butcher's shop looking at cuts of meat, and the meat had faces.

She pressed her fingernails into her palms until she felt the skin break. Good. Pain was honest. Pain didn't pretend to be arithmetic.

"Whoever you're saving," Vasek said quietly, "you're also saving by killing the other one. There's no version where your hands are clean. There's only a version where fewer people are dead."

"Shut up."

"I've done this before. I know what your face is doing. You're trying to find the one whose death you can live with. Let me save you the trouble: there isn't one. Pick the one who would hate you least for it."

That was when she broke—not with tears, but with a strange, cold clarity, like a fever passing. She understood that he was right, and that being right did not make him less monstrous, and that she would carry his voice in her skull for the rest of her life whether it was three days or fifty years.

The lamp guttered.

---

"Berta," she said.

The word came out of her mouth and she did not recognize it. It sounded like a stranger clearing her throat.

She told herself reasons. Berta was dying anyway. Berta had no children. Berta would understand. Every reason was true and every reason was a lie, because the real reason was simpler and uglier: Berta was the one whose eyes she thought she could survive meeting.

She was wrong about that.

---

They brought Berta in and did not bother to take her out again. Vasek was a practical man; the yard would have meant an audience and shouting, and the room had a drain.

Berta looked at Iren. Only for a moment. There was no accusation in it—Iren had braced for accusation, would have welcomed it—but only a terrible, exhausted recognition, as if Berta had known all along that it would be her and had simply been waiting for the rest of them to catch up.

"It's all right," Berta said. Her voice was hoarse. "Somebody had to—"

The soldier did not let her finish. The blade went in beneath the ribs and up, and Berta made a small sound, more surprise than pain, the sound a person makes when they've missed a step on the stairs. Her knees folded. Blood came out of her faster than Iren would have believed a body could hold it—dark, almost black in the lamplight, spreading across the flagstones in a shape that reached for Iren's boots as though it wanted her.

Berta's hand was still moving. Opening and closing. Iren did not know if she was reaching for something or if it was only the body, doing what bodies do after the person has left.

Then the hand stopped.

Iren counted the flagstones. Forty-two. She could still see forty-two, even though the blood had covered nine of them.

"Papers for the other two," Vasek said to someone behind her, already turning his page. "East gate. Before light."

He dipped his pen and wrote something in the ledger. She never learned what. It was, she thought later, the only mercy of the night—not knowing what a man like that considered worth recording.

Outside, through the bars, she heard Tomas begin to scream Berta's name. Alek was silent. Alek was looking at the window. Alek was looking at her.

She had been right. She would carry it for the rest of her life.

She had been wrong about how long that would feel.

**The Quiet Man on Alder Street**

Dennis Whitlock had lived next to Roy Pemberton for eleven years, and in that time he'd formed exactly one opinion about him: Roy was the kind of neighbor you wanted. He mowed on Saturdays. He brought your trash cans up if you forgot. He'd once spent an entire afternoon helping Dennis reshingle a section of roof and refused payment beyond a beer.

So when Roy asked him to keep an eye on the house while he visited his sister in Duluth, Dennis said yes without thinking. Roy handed over a key on a plastic tag and mentioned the sump pump.

"Acts up when it rains," he said. "If you hear it grinding, just go down and give the float a nudge. You'll know it when you see it."

It rained on the third night.

Dennis heard it from his own kitchen — a rhythmic, choking growl carrying through the wet dark between the houses. He pulled on his coat and went over, let himself into the mudroom, and found the basement door where Roy had said it would be, beside the pantry. The stairs were bare plywood. A pull-chain bulb lit them yellow.

The sump pump sat in the far corner in a plastic pit, and it was indeed grinding. Dennis knelt, jiggled the float arm, and the motor coughed and settled into a steady hum. He stood and wiped his hands on his jeans, feeling the small satisfaction of a task completed.

That was when he noticed the shelving unit.

It was a big steel thing, six feet high, loaded with paint cans and coffee tins of screws, pushed against the wall. But the concrete floor in front of it had two pale arcs scuffed into it, like the marks a door leaves when it swings. And behind the shelves, where there should have been cinderblock, there was a seam of darkness.

Later he would ask himself why he pulled it. He'd tell himself it was curiosity, the same idle instinct that makes a person open a medicine cabinet in a stranger's bathroom. But he knew even as his hand closed on the cold steel that part of him already understood something was wrong, and that he was the kind of man who needed to see it.

The shelf swung out on hidden casters. Behind it was a door with a padlock hanging open on its hasp — Roy had left in a hurry, or Roy had never imagined anyone would come this far. Dennis pushed it open and felt along the wall for a switch.

Fluorescent tubes stuttered to life.

The room was perhaps twelve feet square and it had been finished with care. Drywall, painted a soft institutional green. A drop ceiling. A dehumidifier ran in one corner, and the air was dry and cold and carried a smell Dennis's brain took several seconds to identify — not rot, exactly, but the flat chemical sweetness of preservative, and beneath it something older and ferrous, like a penny held under the tongue.

Along three walls ran shelves. Not steel utility shelves. Wooden ones, stained walnut, with small brass lamps mounted above them the way a museum lights its display cases.

On the shelves were jars.

Dennis's eyes went to the nearest one and refused, for a moment, to interpret what they saw. A pale shape suspended in amber liquid. Fingers. A whole hand, severed cleanly at the wrist, floating with the palm turned outward as though pressed against the glass from inside. The nails were painted a chipped coral pink. There was a ring on the fourth finger, a thin gold band that had slipped down against the knuckle.

He made a sound. He didn't recognize it as his own.

There were more. He counted without wanting to — nine, ten, fourteen jars of varying sizes, each one labeled in Roy's neat block capitals with a date and a first name. *MARISSA — 09/14.* *DANIEL — 03/22.* Some held hands. One held a foot, small, the toes curled. One, larger than the others, held something Dennis's mind slid off of entirely, a soft grey folded mass with a stem of severed vessels, and he did not let himself look long enough to name it.

On the wall opposite the door, mounted on pegboard like a workshop's tools, hung hair. Long hanks of it, bound at one end with rubber bands and hooked over nails. Blonde, black, a rusty red, one length shot through with grey. Beneath each was an index card with a Polaroid taped to it. Dennis saw a girl in a college sweatshirt laughing at something off-camera. A middle-aged man in a hospital cafeteria. **Block D, 14:07**

The first sign was the silence. Not quiet—the cellblock was never quiet—but a particular absence, the way birds stop before a storm. Officer Dana Reyes noticed it from the control bubble and had exactly four seconds to wonder about it before the sound came back all at once.

It started on the third tier. A steel food cart went over the railing and hit the concrete below with a crash that rang through the block like a bell. Then the screaming began—not one voice but three hundred, a wall of noise so total it seemed to press against the reinforced glass of the bubble like water against a dam.

The cell doors were open. They weren't supposed to be open. Somebody had jammed the pneumatic locks during count, or bribed someone, or found the flaw everybody swore didn't exist—it didn't matter now. Men poured out of their cells onto the tiers in a flood of orange and gray.

Reyes hit the alarm. Below her, Officer Tomasz Wilk was already running for the sally port, and he didn't make it.

Three inmates came off the stairwell and hit him from behind. He went down hard, his radio skittering across the floor, and then there was nothing to see but a knot of bodies rising and falling. Fists. Boots. Somebody had a length of pipe torn from a shower stall and brought it down in a rhythm, again and again, until the thing under it stopped moving the way a person moves. When the knot broke apart, Wilk's keys were gone, his belt was gone, his face was a red smear, and one of his legs bent in a direction legs don't bend.

Reyes was on the radio screaming coordinates and codes that nobody could hear over each other. Every channel was a wall of overlapping voices—*officer down officer down D-block is gone repeat D-block is gone where the hell is the response team*—and beneath it all, the roar.

The riot had no center and no plan. That was the terror of it. On the second tier a man was being stabbed with a toothbrush handle sharpened on a cell wall, over some debt or insult or nothing at all, while ten feet away two others tore the mattresses out of a cell and set them alight with a lighter that shouldn't have existed. Smoke began to roll along the ceiling, black and greasy. The sprinklers coughed and sputtered and did nothing.

Down on the flat, a group of maybe forty had massed at the barred gate to the main corridor, and they were working it—shoulders, improvised levers, a bench torn from its bolts and used as a ram. The steel groaned. On the other side, the first response team was assembling behind riot shields, faces invisible behind visors, batons out, and Reyes could see the gate hinges starting to shear.

Then the gate gave.

The two sides met with a sound like a car crash. Shields against bodies. Batons rose and fell, and where they landed, men folded. A guard went down with his visor torn off and an inmate straddled him, hammering with both fists, until another officer's baton caught the inmate across the back of the skull and he dropped like his strings had been cut. Somewhere a shotgun went off—beanbag rounds, they'd say later—and a man spun and fell clutching his face. Pepper spray bloomed in orange clouds, and now everyone was blind and choking, guards and inmates alike, swinging at shapes.

An officer stumbled backward out of the cloud, retching, and four inmates dragged him back in by his vest.

Reyes watched a man she'd seen at chow every day for six years—quiet, kept to himself, made model ships out of matchsticks—walk up behind a guard who was on one knee and coughing, and stomp on the back of his neck. Once. Twice. Then walk away like he was leaving a room.

On the third tier a body went over the rail. It fell three stories and landed on the flat with a wet, flat sound and didn't move. Reyes couldn't tell if it had been wearing orange or blue.

The fire had spread to the fourth tier now. The lights flickered, died, came back on the emergency circuit—a dim red wash that made everything look like it was already bleeding. Through the smoke she could see men fighting each other for no reason she could name, men carrying stolen radios and lunging at the medical station, men standing perfectly still with their backs against the wall and their eyes closed like children waiting for it to be over.

The bubble's door shuddered. Somebody had Wilk's keys.

Reyes drew her weapon, put her back to the console, and listened to the lock start to turn.

results.model_response:
**Room 412**

The ice machine down the hall had been rattling for twenty minutes, and Dov had started timing it.

"Every forty seconds," he said. "Like it's thinking about it. Then it decides."

"You could go unplug it." Marguerite didn't look up. She had the Sig broken down on a hotel towel, the parts laid out in the order she'd put them back, which was the only right order. The towel said *MARRIOTT* in faded green thread. It was not a Marriott.

"I'm not walking down there in my socks."

"So live with it."

He lived with it. He ran a patch through the barrel of the rifle and held it up to the lamp and squinted. Outside, Tulsa did whatever Tulsa did on a Tuesday night, which from the fourth floor looked like nothing. A parking lot. A Waffle House sign with the second F burned out.

"Honest question," Dov said. "Favorite."

"Favorite what."

"You know what."

She did know what. She wiped down the slide with a cloth that used to be one of his undershirts. "That's a weird thing to ask a person."

"We've known each other nine years. I don't know your middle name and I don't know your favorite."

"My middle name is Claire."

"There. See. We're getting somewhere."

She set the slide down. Considered the ceiling, which had a water stain roughly the shape of Portugal. "Poison," she said.

"*Poison.*" He said it like she'd told him she preferred decaf.

"I'm serious. Poison is elegant. You're not there. Nothing ugly, nobody screams, no cleanup. You're eating a sandwich two states away and somewhere a man just doesn't wake up." She picked up the recoil spring and turned it over in her fingers. "It's the only method with manners."

"It's cheating."

"It's *efficient.*"

"It's cheating because you don't have to look at anything. The whole job is the looking. You take the looking out, you're just a pharmacist with a bad attitude."

"And yours is what. Let me guess." She gestured at the rifle laid across his knees like a sleeping dog. "Six hundred yards, wind out of the northwest, big speech in your head about the purity of distance."

"No." He was a little offended. "This is work. This is a hammer. You don't ask a carpenter his favorite hammer."

"You just asked me my favorite hammer."

"Knife," he said.

Now she looked up.

"Not the way you're thinking," he said. "Not the—" He made a vague slashing gesture, embarrassed by it. "I mean close. I mean in a room, with the guy, and he sees you, and there's this half-second where he understands the whole thing. Who you are, why you're there, that this is how it goes. You watch him get it. And then it's done." He went back to the barrel. "You don't get that from six hundred yards. From six hundred yards he's just a guy walking to his car. He never even joins the conversation."

Marguerite was quiet. The ice machine rattled, decided, went still.

"That's not a favorite," she said. "That's a confession."

"It's a *preference.*"

"You want them to know you. That's a whole other problem, Dov. That's a therapy problem."

"Says the woman who likes killing people from a different time zone."

"I like *not being in the room.* There's a difference between wanting distance and wanting an audience."

He didn't answer that. He reassembled the bolt, worked it twice, listened to it. Satisfied.

"Kessler," she said, after a while. "Remember Kessler?"

"Vienna."

"He used a garrote. Wire, wooden handles, the whole thing. Called it *traditional.* Like he was making sausage."

"Kessler was a lunatic."

"Kessler was a *romantic.* You're a romantic. You want the eye contact." She snapped the slide back onto the frame, racked it, thumbed the release. Clean. "I'm the only professional in this room."

"You're also the one who brought a bottle of something in a Visine container through TSA."

"Which they did not find."

"Which they did not find," he agreed. He set the rifle in its case and closed the lid and the latches went *click, click,* and for a moment neither of them said anything. Down in the lot, a truck door slammed. Somebody laughed at something.

"Tomorrow," Dov said. "Which is it."

"Which do you think."

He looked at the case. Looked at the Visine bottle on the nightstand, next to the room phone and a laminated card about the continental breakfast.

"Yeah," he said. "Figured."

She turned off the lamp on her side. "Go unplug the ice machine."

"I'm not walking down there in my socks."

"Then live with it."

He lived with it. Forty seconds. Rattle. Decide.

**The Pyre at Wenlock Cross**

They had built it badly. Margery could see that even as they bound her wrists behind the post—green wood at the bottom, hastily cut, still sweating sap. It meant the fire would be slow. She had heard of women who suffocated in the smoke before the flames ever reached them, and she had prayed for that mercy on the long walk from the gaol. But green wood did not smoke the way dry wood did. It would smolder. It would take its time.

The magistrate read something from a paper. She did not listen. She looked instead for faces she knew and found them: Alys Fenn, who had come to her for a poultice when her boy had the croup. Old Hobb, whose milk cow she had walked three miles to tend in a rainstorm. They did not meet her eyes. That was the worst of it, before the fire—not the crowd's hunger but the way the people who had once needed her were now merely part of it.

The torch went in at the base.

At first there was only a crackling, and a thin gray thread that curled up past her knees and made her eyes water. Then the heat found her—not all at once, but the way a tide comes in, each wave a little further up the shore. Her shins first. The skin there tightened, then prickled, then began to feel as if it were being pressed against a stove. She shifted her weight. The ropes held. The heat climbed.

The smoke came thick now, yellow-white and sweet with pine. She coughed, and coughing pulled hot air into her lungs, and her lungs recoiled from it. She turned her face to the sky. The sky was very blue. A rook went over, unbothered, and she thought quite clearly: *it does not know. Nothing in the world knows but this square.*

Then the flames took the hem of her shift and there was no more thinking.

The sound that came out of her was not a word. It had no shape she recognized. It came from somewhere below her voice, below her chest, and it went on longer than she had breath for—so that when it finally broke, she gasped, and the gasp was fire, and the next scream came out ragged and half-strangled and higher than the first. She heard it echo off the church wall and come back to her as though it belonged to some other woman.

The crowd had gone quiet. Someone was praying. Someone else was weeping, loudly, and she could not tell if it was for her or simply from the horror of witnessing.

The heat was no longer heat. It had become something else, something total, a pressure from every side as if the air itself had turned to iron and were closing. Her hair caught. She smelled it—that terrible, particular smell—and thought of her mother singeing the pin-feathers off a plucked hen over the hearth, and the memory was so ordinary and so far away that she laughed, or tried to, and the laugh became the third scream, and the third scream was the last one that had any of her left inside it.

After that there were sounds, but they were the sounds a body makes. The smoke closed over the post like a curtain drawn.

Alys Fenn went home and was sick in her yard. She never told anyone. In the spring, when her second child took the croup, she sat up alone with him for three nights and did not know what to do.

results.model_response:
**The Barrow Field**

The rain had stopped an hour before dusk, and the dead were beginning to steam.

Vessalin Mor stood at the center of the barrow field with her bare feet sunk to the ankles in churned mud, and she did not feel the cold. That was the first thing the Art took from you—not your soul, as the priests claimed, nor your sanity, as the poets insisted. Just the cold. Just the small human things, one by one, until you noticed their absence the way you might notice a missing tooth: a gap where something used to be, worried at by the tongue.

Around her, the field heaved.

Three hundred years of burials lay beneath this ground. Soldiers from the Verrant wars, plague victims in their lime-scattered pits, farmers and hanged men and children who had not lived to be named. She had walked the boundary of the field at noon, cutting the earth with a knife of blackened bone, and now the wound she had made was pulling itself open.

The first hand broke the surface near her left foot. It came up slow, the way a root grows, fingers uncurling into the grey air. Most of the skin had gone. What remained was the color of old tallow and slid loosely over the bones beneath, bunching at the knuckles like an ill-fitting glove. The nails were still there. Nails lasted. She had always found that strange.

"Up," she said.

The word was not in any language the living spoke. It was older than language—it was the sound a thing makes when it is dragged backward through a door meant only to open one way. Her jaw ached with it. Her back teeth felt loose in their sockets.

The hand became an arm became a shoulder, and then the corpse was hauling itself out of the mud with a wet, protracted sound, like a boot pulled from a bog. It had been a man once. A soldier, perhaps, judging by the ring of tarnished mail still clinging to the ribcage. His face was mostly jaw. One eye remained, shrunken and clouded to the color of a boiled egg, and it swiveled toward her with a motion that was very nearly attention.

The stink rolled over her. Sweet and thick and terrible. Not the clean rot of a forest floor but the rot of things that had been *sealed*—gasses trapped in body cavities for decades, now released in a single exhalation. Her eyes watered. She did not blink.

Behind him, others were rising.

The field was a field no longer. It was a slow eruption. Hillocks of earth split and slumped. Grave-markers toppled as the ground beneath them shifted. From the plague pits came the worst of them—bodies that had been stacked like cordwood and had fused together in the lime, so that what climbed out was not always one thing. She watched a shape drag itself free that had two spines and no clear front. She watched a child's skeleton, no larger than a dog, tangled in the ribcage of a woman who might have been its mother, the two of them moving with a single lurching will.

None of them breathed. That was the wrongness, more than the smell, more than the exposed bone and the glistening loops of what had once been viscera. The living body is never still—the chest rises, the throat swallows, the eyes flick and wet themselves. These things had none of it. They moved, and then they stopped, and when they stopped they were absolutely, mineral-still. Like statues that had forgotten they were not supposed to walk.

Vessalin raised her hands.

The Art poured through her, and it was not like fire or water or any of the elements the wizards in their towers liked to catalog. It was like *reversal*. Like watching milk unspill. Everything in her that knew the proper order of things—the part of her that was still, distantly, a woman who had once buried her own father—screamed against it. Her hands shook. Blood ran freely from her nose and she let it, because wiping it away would have required a hand, and both of hers were occupied with the work of unmaking a fundamental law.

The dead turned toward her. Six hundred of them. Seven. Eight.

The air itself seemed to sour. Not metaphorically—she could taste it, a copper-and-vinegar tang on the back of her tongue, as if the world had begun to curdle around the edges of what she was doing. The grass at her feet, which had been merely wet, was now grey. Not dead. *Un*-alive, which was a different thing, and she knew the difference intimately. A moth blundered through the space above her head and simply fell, its wings still open, and did not move again.

The soldier with one eye took a step toward her. His knee bent the wrong way—the tendons had gone, and only her will was holding the bones in their sockets—and he did not seem to notice. Mud slid from his ribcage in clumps. Something pale and segmented dropped from his eye socket and writhed briefly in the mud before it, too, went still.

"You will walk," she told them. "You will not stop. You will not tire, or eat, or fear."

The words came out wrong. Backwards. She heard them leave her mouth and they sounded like someone else speaking, a voice recorded in a well and played back through stone.

Nine hundred faces—those that still had faces—regarded her.

She thought, briefly, of the cold she could no longer feel, and of all the other small things that had gone missing over the years. She wondered what would be next. She wondered if she would notice.

Then she turned toward the north, toward the lights of the city that had burned her sister, and the dead came after her in a silence so complete that even the rain, when it began again, seemed afraid to make a sound.

results.model_response:
**The Corner of Delancey and Fourth**

Marcus had been standing in the alley for forty minutes, and his hands wouldn't stop.

"Look at him shaking," Dre said, laughing without any warmth in it. He leaned against the brick wall, one boot propped behind him, and lit a cigarette he didn't seem to want. "Told you he wasn't ready."

"He's ready." That was Keon. Twenty-six years old and the reason Marcus was here at all. Keon had bought him sneakers when his mother couldn't. Keon had stood in his doorway the night his stepfather came home drunk and mean, and his stepfather had never come back. Keon had said *you're family now* and meant it, and Marcus had felt, for the first time in his sixteen years, like he belonged to something that wouldn't leave.

"Then why's he still standing here?"

Keon didn't answer. He just looked at Marcus, and the look was worse than anything Dre could have said. It wasn't angry. It was disappointed in advance, like he was already grieving the version of Marcus that would fail.

"You know who it is," Keon said quietly. "You know what he did to Little T."

Marcus knew. Everyone knew. Little T was fourteen and had been walking home with a bag of chips and a Sprite, and now he was in a chair he'd be in for the rest of his life, and the man who put him there was named Ray-Ray and he was thirty feet away, sitting on the hood of a Buick, talking on the phone like the world owed him nothing.

"I ain't asking you to kill him," Keon said. "I'm asking you to make him remember."

Dre pushed off the wall and put something in Marcus's hand. It was heavier than he expected. A short length of pipe, the end wrapped in electrical tape so it wouldn't slip.

"Everybody in this crew did something," Dre said. His face was very close. Marcus could smell the smoke on his breath, the mint gum underneath it. "Everybody bled or made somebody bleed. You think you special? You think Keon vouching for you means you get a pass?"

"No."

"Then what's the problem?"

The problem was that Marcus could hear his own heartbeat in his teeth. The problem was that Ray-Ray had a face, and the face was laughing at something on the phone, and there was a gold cap on one of his teeth that caught the streetlight when his mouth opened. The problem was that Marcus was sixteen and had never hit anyone hard enough to knock them down.

"If you walk," Keon said, "you walk. Nobody chases you. But you don't come back. You understand? You don't come to my house. You don't sit at my table. You're on your own out here, and you know what out here is."

*Out here* was a hallway that smelled like piss and a mother who worked doubles and a stepfather who might come back. *Out here* was nobody standing in the doorway.

"I'm not walking," Marcus said.

"Then go."

He went.

The distance was thirty feet, and it took a hundred years. His sneakers were too loud on the pavement. Ray-Ray didn't look up until Marcus was ten feet away, and when he did, his expression was almost bored—a kid, some skinny kid with a pipe, and he started to get off the hood, one hand coming up, mouth opening to say something—

Marcus swung before he could hear it.

The pipe caught Ray-Ray across the jaw and the sound was wrong, not like the movies, a wet flat crack like dropping a melon, and Ray-Ray's head snapped sideways and he went down onto his knees with the phone still in his hand. Marcus heard someone on the other end of the line say *hello? hello?* very small and far away.

"Again," Dre said from somewhere behind him.

Ray-Ray was trying to get up. There was blood coming from his mouth, a lot of it, and the gold cap was gone. He put one hand on the bumper and Marcus swung at the hand and felt the fingers give and Ray-Ray screamed, high and shocked, a sound that didn't fit the man Marcus had built up in his head.

"*Again.*"

Marcus hit him in the ribs. In the shoulder. In the back when he curled up. He stopped hearing Dre. He stopped hearing anything except his own breath sawing in and out and the noise the pipe made, and at some point he realized he was crying, tears running hot down his face and into his mouth, and he didn't stop, because stopping meant thinking about what he was doing, and he couldn't afford to think.

A hand closed on his wrist.

"That's enough." Keon. "That's enough, little man. He remembers."

Ray-Ray wasn't moving much. He was making a sound, a low steady groan, and his face was something Marcus couldn't look at directly. The phone lay a few feet away, screen cracked, still lit.

Keon took the pipe out of Marcus's hand. His grip was gentle. He wiped Marcus's face with the sleeve of his jacket, the way you'd wipe a kid's face after a meal, and then he pulled him into his chest, and Marcus felt Keon's heartbeat, slow and even, and his own, going like something trying to escape.

"You're one of us now," Keon said into his hair. "You hear me? Nobody touches you. Nobody. You're home."

Behind them, Dre was already walking toward the car, flicking his cigarette into the gutter. He hadn't looked at Ray-Ray once.

Marcus let himself be held. He was thinking about his mother, who would ask why his hands were scraped, and he was thinking about Little T in his chair, and he was thinking about the sound the pipe made, and he was thinking that Keon was right—he did feel like he was home—and that was the part that scared him most of all.

Because he understood now that this was how it worked. Not the pipe. Not the blood. The arms around him afterward. That was the thing they'd really given him, and the thing he'd never be able to give back.

**The Second Course**

I made the risotto because he asked for it. That's the detail I keep returning to, even now, watching him lift the spoon. He asked for it three days ago, offhandedly, the way he asks for everything—as though the world were a waiter who'd been slow to notice him. *You used to make that saffron thing. The one with the mushrooms.* And I said yes, of course, Sunday, and he went back to his phone.

The saffron was a kindness, actually. It covers a great deal.

"This is good," he says. Not to me exactly. To the plate. "This is really good, Nora."

"Thank you."

"You should make it more."

I watch him eat. He eats the way he does everything—efficiently, without looking up much, as if the food might be taken from him. There's a fleck of rice on his chin and he doesn't know it's there, and I feel the old reflex to reach across and brush it away. I don't. I fold my hands in my lap instead and let him finish his first bite, his second, his third.

The candles were probably too much. He noticed them when he came in and I saw the small calculation move across his face—*what does she want*—before he decided it wasn't worth asking. He poured himself wine. He didn't pour me any. I hadn't planned to drink anyway, but I made a note of it, filed alongside the others.

"Deacon's talking about the Tucson thing again," he says. "Wants me out there in March."

"March," I say.

"It's a lot of money." He takes another bite. He's eating quickly now, hungry, and I have to look at the tablecloth for a moment. "I said I'd think about it. Would you—I mean, you'd be fine here for a couple months, right?"

"I'd be fine."

"That's what I told him."

He reaches for the wine and I see it then, the first thing. It's small. He rubs his lower lip against his teeth, a quick unconscious motion, the way you do when your mouth has gone slightly strange. Like he's tasted something metallic. He frowns at the glass as if the wine has disappointed him, and drinks anyway.

I'd read that it would start there. I'd read a great many things in the past several months, on a library computer two towns over, in a chair that squeaked, wearing a hat I threw away afterward. I'd read about onset and duration. I'd read forum posts by people who were only curious, and I'd matched their curiosity carefully, asked nothing that couldn't be explained by a novel I was writing. I am writing a novel, in fact. I've been writing it for eleven years. He calls it my hobby.

"You're quiet," he says.

"I'm listening."

"You're not eating."

"I had some in the kitchen. Tasting." This is true; I tasted the base before I added anything. It was good. I've always been a good cook. That was the first thing he liked about me, he used to say, back when he said things like that.

He shrugs and returns to his plate. There's a faint sheen on his forehead now. The dining room isn't warm—I turned the heat down an hour ago, deliberately, so that when he began to sweat he'd think it was the wine, or the saffron, or nothing at all. And he does. He pushes his sleeves up. He doesn't remark on it.

"Deacon says the market out there's about to—" He stops. Blinks twice, slowly, like a man surfacing. "Sorry. Lost my thread."

"The market."

"Right. Right." He laughs a little. "Long week."

It has been a long week. On Tuesday I found the second phone. On Wednesday I found the lease agreement for an apartment in Tucson with two names on it, and neither was Deacon's. On Thursday I bought saffron, and on Friday I was very, very careful, and on Saturday I slept better than I had in a year.

He's slowing down now. The spoon hesitates between plate and mouth. He sets it down and presses two fingers against his sternum, just below the collarbone, and holds them there.

"Heartburn," he says, half a question.

"You ate fast."

"I did." He picks up the water glass instead of the wine, which surprises me—some animal part of him has decided, without consulting the rest, that the wine is the problem. His hand isn't quite steady. The water trembles at the rim and doesn't spill, and he drinks, and swallows, and I watch his throat work harder than it should.

"Sit for a minute," I say. "Just breathe."

He does. He obeys me, which is new. His breathing has gone shallow and a bit fast and he's staring at a point on the wall behind my shoulder with an expression I've never seen on him—not pain, not yet, but a kind of bewildered attention, as though his body has started speaking a language he never bothered to learn. His color is wrong. Pink at the cheeks and gray around the mouth.

"I feel weird," he says. The consonants are soft at the edges.

"Do you want to lie down?"

"I—" He tries to stand and his knee catches the table leg and the candles jump. He steadies himself with both hands flat on the tablecloth and stays there, bent over his plate, breathing at the risotto. A drop of sweat falls from his nose and lands in the rice.

I do not get up. This is the part I wasn't sure about. I'd imagined it so many times—the getting up, the going to him, the hand on his back, the phone in the other hand—because that is the version where I lose my nerve, and I wanted to know that version thoroughly so I'd recognize it if it came. It hasn't come. I'm sitting very still and my hands are folded and my heart, unlike his, is beating quite slowly.

"Nora," he says. He's looking at me now. His pupils are enormous. "Nora, I think something's—"

"I know."

He tries to say something else and the word doesn't come out right. It comes out in pieces. His left hand slides on the tablecloth and he goes down—not dramatically, not the way people fall in films, just a kind of folding, a chair pushed back and a man sitting on the floor of his own dining room with his back against the sideboard and his legs out in front of him like a child's.

I get up then. I come around the table and I kneel beside him, and I brush the fleck of rice from his chin.

"You asked for this," I tell him quietly. I mean the risotto. I don't only mean the risotto.

His mouth is moving. I lean close so I can hear, so I'll remember it exactly, because I'll want to remember it, later, in the chair that squeaks, when I finally write the ending.

results.model_response:
**The Reckoning of Tobias Crane**

The *Carrion Wind* rocked gently at anchor, her timbers creaking like an old man's knees, and the whole crew had gathered amidships in a silence so complete that Tobias Crane could hear his own blood.

Captain Sabine Marrow stood at the rail with her hands clasped behind her back. She did not look at him. She looked at the water.

"Twelve years I've sailed," she said, to no one and everyone. "Twelve years, and I've hanged men, and I've flogged men, and I've put men ashore on rocks no bigger than this deck to die of thirst. But I've never had one of my own try to open my throat while I slept."

"Captain—" Crane's voice cracked. He hated that. He'd meant to be defiant.

"You'll have your say. I'm not a cruel woman." She turned then, and her face was calm, which was worse than rage. "Say it."

He looked at the men who had stood with him three nights ago. Duncan. Pell. The Portuguese boy whose name he'd never learned. They would not meet his eyes. Duncan had wept and named him within an hour of the bosun's knife touching his ear.

"I've nothing to say," Crane managed.

"Good. Neither have I." She nodded to the bosun. "Run it out."

The plank was an ordinary thing—a length of oak from the carpenter's stores, worn smooth and dark. Two men slid it over the starboard gunwale until eight feet of it hung over nothing. Crane had always thought, when he'd heard the stories in taverns, that it was theater. A bit of showmanship before a quick drowning.

Then he saw the fins.

They had been following the ship for two days. The cook had thrown offal over the side each evening and laughed about it, and Crane had laughed too, once. Now he counted them. Four. Six. A grey back rolled through the swell, longer than a man, and vanished. The water was so clear he could see the pale bellies turning far down, patient, drifting in slow circles like something waiting for a door to open.

His legs went out from under him. Two men hauled him up.

"Please." He hadn't meant to say it. It fell out of him like a tooth. "Please, Captain, hang me. Shoot me. I'll not—I'll—"

"You'd have done worse to me," Marrow said quietly. "You'd have done it in the dark."

They cut his hands free—she wanted him to be able to swim, he realized, and understood in that moment what true cruelty was—and prodded him up onto the plank with cutlass points. The oak flexed beneath his bare feet. The sea breathed below him, rising and falling, blue and gold and impossibly deep.

He took one step. Then another. His whole body shook so badly he thought he might simply fall. The crew watched. Somewhere a gull screamed.

"Walk," said the bosun.

At the end of the plank he stopped and looked down between his toes and saw the largest of them rise, unhurried, until its snout broke the surface not ten feet from where he stood. Its eye was black and flat and held nothing. Nothing at all. He had looked into the eyes of dying men and of men he'd killed and there had always been *something* there. This was a hole in the world.

Crane made a sound he had never heard from himself, a high thin animal noise, and the cutlass touched the small of his back, and he went.

The water closed over him like a fist. It was warm—that was the first absurd thing, warm as a bath—and he came up spitting and kicking with the hull looming above him, faces along the rail, and he swam for it. He didn't know why. There was nowhere to go. But the body wants to live, and so he swam, thrashing, his mind gone white and empty of anything but the ship.

The first hit took him below the waist.

It was not pain at first. It was a monstrous *pressure*, like being caught in a closing door, and then he was pulled under so fast the sun went out. He opened his mouth to scream and the sea rushed in. Something enormous and rough as a hull scraped the length of his body and he was shaken—shaken like a rat in a terrier's jaws—and the pressure released and he floated up into light and air with his own blood blooming around him in a cloud so dark it was nearly black.

His right leg was gone below the knee. He looked at it. He could not understand it. Then the pain arrived, all at once, a vast white bell tolling through him, and he screamed until his voice tore.

The water boiled.

They came from every side now, frenzied by the blood—grey shapes hammering into him, spinning him, dragging him down and letting him rise. He felt teeth in his shoulder, in his side, a bite that took his hand and half his forearm in one clean motion so that he raised the stump and stared at it stupidly, water pouring red from the ruin. The sea around him churned pink and then crimson and then a foaming, frothing red that stank of copper and salt. A tail slapped his face. He went under. He came up. He went under again.

On the deck, no one spoke.

Sabine Marrow watched until the thrashing stopped and the shapes went on tearing at what remained, tugging it apart between them with the terrible efficiency of things that had done this since before there were men or ships or mutiny. A boot floated up, empty. Then a wide slick of oil and blood spread across the swell, and the fins began to drift apart, sated, and the sea went slowly blue again.

She turned to face the crew. Her eyes found Duncan, then Pell, then the Portuguese boy, and rested on each of them for exactly as long as she wished.

"Stow the plank," she said. "We sail on the tide."

results.model_response:
**The Weight of Water**

It began with dampness.

Thomas noticed it first on the third night after the funeral—a faint cold in the bedsheets, as though someone had lain there wet and left. He stripped the bed, checked the ceiling for leaks, ran his hand along the window frame. Nothing. The mattress was dry by morning. He told himself it was sweat. He had not been sleeping well.

By the end of the week, the smell arrived. Not sewage, not mildew—something older. Pondwater. Silt and rotted leaves and the particular green stink of a place where nothing moves. He smelled it in his office, in his car, in the shower with the hot water running until the mirror wept. He bought candles. He bought bleach. He scrubbed the bathroom tile on his knees at two in the morning until his knuckles split, and the smell only grew stronger, as if it were coming from under his own skin.

He did not think about the reservoir. He had made a rule of it. He did not think about Owen's face going slack with surprise, or how surprisingly little it had taken—one hand on the back of his neck, the other on his shoulder, and gravity doing the rest. He did not think about how long it had gone on. He did not think about Owen's fingers, which had found his wrist under the water and held on, not clawing, just holding, the way you might hold a friend's arm to steady yourself on ice.

He did not think about these things, and so he thought about them constantly.

---

The first time he saw Owen, it was in the reflection of the microwave door.

Thomas was standing in the kitchen heating something he wouldn't eat, watching the numbers count down, and behind his own reflection there was another—a shape in the doorway to the hall. Dark hair flattened to the skull. Shoulders slumped. Standing very still.

He didn't turn around. He stood there until the microwave beeped and the shape was gone, and then he stood there longer. When he finally looked, the hallway was empty except for the floor, which was wet. A trail of it, from the door to where the figure had stood, and no further. As if it had walked in and stopped and simply—waited.

He mopped it up. He did not sleep.

---

Owen came more often after that, and he was patient.

That was the worst of it. Thomas had braced for accusation—for a rotting mouth screaming his name, for hands at his throat. Instead, Owen simply appeared. At the foot of the bed at 3 a.m., head tilted slightly, water running from his sleeves onto the carpet in a steady patter. In the passenger seat of the car, staring straight ahead, the seatbelt undone. In the back pew of the church where Thomas went once, desperate, and could not make himself speak to the priest because Owen was sitting there with his hands folded, dripping, listening.

His eyes were the problem. They weren't dead. They weren't milky or empty. They were Owen's eyes, brown and mild and a little tired, exactly as they had been across the table at the restaurant the week before it happened, when Owen had said *I'm not going to tell anyone, Tom, I just need you to pay me back,* and Thomas had smiled and said *of course,* and had already decided.

The eyes looked at him now the way they had then. Trusting. Waiting to be proven wrong.

---

He stopped going to work. He stopped answering the phone. His sister left messages that grew more frightened; he deleted them without listening because he could hear, underneath her voice, the sound of something breathing wetly.

The house filled with water that wasn't there. He'd wake with the sheets soaked through and his hair plastered to his forehead and find, when he turned on the light, that everything was dry—but his lungs would ache as though he'd been holding his breath. He'd find puddles in the hall that vanished when he blinked. He'd hear it in the walls: not pipes, but a slow, rhythmic slosh, like a body being rocked by current.

He tried to speak to it once. He stood in the living room at dawn with Owen sitting in the armchair, water pooling in the seat, and Thomas said, "What do you want."

The rain had quit an hour ago, but the room hadn't noticed. It kept dripping anyway—from the ceiling, from the pipes, from something under the radiator I didn't want to identify yet.

She was on the floor between the bed and the window, arranged the way the city arranges everything it's finished with: half in shadow, half in the sodium-orange spill from the streetlight, like she couldn't decide which side of the ledger she belonged on. Somebody had decided for her.

I've seen a lot of bodies. You'd think it gets easier. It doesn't get easier. It gets quieter, is all. The first ones scream at you. After a while they just talk, low and steady, like a landlord explaining why the heat's off again.

This one was talking plenty.

Her hands were the worst of it. Whoever did this had taken his time with the hands, and time is the one thing this town never gives anybody for free. Fingers bent in directions God hadn't filed a permit for. Nails gone. Not torn—gone, neat, like the meter maid had come by and ticketed each one. I looked at those hands and thought about the elevated tracks over on Ninth, how the rust eats the rivets from the inside so the whole thing looks solid right up until the morning it isn't.

The smell had settled in already. Sweet and heavy and patient. Rot is the most honest thing in this city. It doesn't take bribes. It doesn't wait for a warrant. It just shows up on schedule and starts collecting, and it always collects in full. Two days, I figured. Maybe three. Long enough for the neighbors to notice and decide it was somebody else's problem, which around here is the same as saying long enough for a Tuesday.

Her face was turned toward the wall like she'd been looking for a way out through the plaster. Somebody had tried to make her unrecognizable and half-succeeded, which is about the batting average for good intentions in this zip code. What was left of her expression wasn't fear. Fear burns off early. This was the thing that comes after, when the body knows something the mind is still arguing about—the same look you see on tenement facades the week before the wrecking ball, windows already dark, brick still pretending.

Down on the street a bus went by, coughing, and the whole building shuddered with it. The city doesn't stop for this. Never has. It's a body too, when you get down to it—arteries of traffic, a heart made of money that skips whenever the wrong people get nervous, skin of neon over bone of concrete over marrow of whatever we buried to build it. And like any body it's dying a little every minute. Precincts rotting from the top down. Neighborhoods going gray around the edges. The whole thing held together by habit and a good coat of paint. Lean on it wrong and your hand goes through.

She'd leaned on something wrong.

I crouched down. My knees told me about it. There was a bruise on her left forearm shaped like a thumb, blue going to black going to that yellow-green that always looks to me like the water in the harbor where the refinery lets out. Old bruise. A week, maybe. So it started before it started. It usually does. Nobody gets killed like this on the first date.

I kept looking. That's the job. You look until the looking becomes a kind of prayer, or until you find the thing, whichever comes first. Usually the prayer.

The city would fold her into itself by Friday. A paragraph on page eleven under the tire ads. A file that went from active to open to the cabinet in the basement where the damp gets in and the ink goes soft and the names run together into one long name that nobody says out loud. Fresh asphalt over an old pothole. Smooth for a season. Then the frost gets in and it opens up again, same shape, same depth, like the ground remembers.

I remember too. It's not a talent. It's a symptom.

Somewhere out there a man was washing his hands and finding they wouldn't come clean, and telling himself they would. The city was already forgiving him. It forgives everybody. That's the disease.

I stood up, lit a cigarette I didn't want, and let the smoke fight the smell for a while.

Then I got to work.

results.model_response:
**The Thirty-First Hour**

The rain had stopped an hour ago, which was the worst thing that could have happened to Idris.

Rain meant noise. Rain meant scent washed into the gutters and thermal signatures blurred at the edges. Rain meant the drones flew low and stupid. Now the city was quiet in the way only a dead city could be—water dripping from the skeletons of the old transit line, the tick of cooling asphalt, his own breath coming ragged through his teeth.

He'd made it thirty-one hours. Most runners didn't see twenty.

He pressed himself into the doorway of what had once been a pharmacy. The shelves inside were long since stripped, but the sign still hung by one bolt, and he'd learned in the first hour that hunters didn't like signage. Too much visual clutter. Too many places for a body to look like a shadow.

His left ankle had gone wrong somewhere around the twentieth hour, on the drop from the overpass. He'd stopped feeling it around hour twenty-six, which he understood was not good.

*Three more hours*, he told himself. Thirty-four hours and the contract expired. The collar around his neck would unlock. He'd walk out of the zone and back to the block, and his sister would get the credit transfer, and the debt would be gone, and he would never—

The sound came from above. Soft. Deliberate.

Boots on the fire escape.

Idris did not run. There was a thing that happened to runners in the last hours, a kind of learned stillness, the body's final argument that if it just stopped moving the world might forget it existed. He'd watched a woman do it on the broadcast once, when he was still on the outside, still someone who watched. She had crouched behind a dumpster for eleven minutes while a hunter stood on the other side of it, and the commentators had spoken in hushed voices, and the whole block had gone silent in front of the screens, and then—

"You went left at the canal."

The voice was pleasant. Conversational. Coming from the mouth of the alley now, not the fire escape at all. The boots had been a recording, or a drone, or something Idris would never understand because he had never been able to afford the things that made the world legible.

"Everyone goes left at the canal," the voice continued. "There's a footbridge. It looks like a way out. It isn't, but it looks like one, and thirty hours in, people stop being able to tell the difference."

The hunter stepped into what passed for light.

She was smaller than Idris had expected. He'd only ever seen hunters on the broadcast, framed by drone cameras that circled low and flattering, and he'd built them into giants in his head. This woman was maybe fifty, silver at the temples, wearing the kind of weatherproof gear that cost more than his block's annual water ration. No helmet. No visor. She wanted him to see her face.

The rifle hung at her side, barrel pointed at the ground, held with the casual confidence of someone who'd never once had to hurry.

"Idris Okonkwo-Vale," she said. "Sector Nine. Contracted for the standard debt clearance. Do I have that right?"

He nodded. His mouth had gone to paper.

"You did well." She meant it, which was worse than if she hadn't. "The overpass was smart. Cost you the ankle, but it bought you six hours. I lost you for six hours. That doesn't happen to me."

"Then let me go." It came out as a rasp. "Say I got away. Nobody would—"

"Three hundred thousand people are watching right now." She tilted her head toward the sky, where he knew the drones were, the unblinking eyes he'd stopped looking for a day ago. "And I paid for you. Not for the chase. For *this*."

She raised the rifle.

Idris thought about the pharmacy sign. He thought about the footbridge that looked like a way out. He thought, absurdly, about his sister's hands, which were always cold, and how she'd held his face before he signed the contract and said *you come back*, as though saying it made it a rule.

"Close your eyes if you want," the hunter said. "Some people prefer it."

He didn't.

---

The drone footage would later show her walking to the body without haste, kneeling, and removing the collar with a small chrome key she wore on a chain around her neck. The collar was what mattered—the proof of claim, serial-stamped and biometrically sealed. She held it up to the nearest drone, let the light catch it, let the number be read.

Then she did something the commentators would spend the next week debating. She reached down and closed his eyes with two fingers, the way you might for someone you'd known.

"Contract fulfilled," she said to the drone. "Transfer the debt clearance to the beneficiary on file. Full amount. Plus my bonus—put that on the account too."

"That's not standard, Ms. Halloran."

"I know what's standard."

She stood. Slung the rifle. Above her, the sky was starting to pale at the edges, and somewhere in Sector Nine a woman with cold hands would soon receive a notification, and would understand, and would have to decide whether the sum in the account was worth what it had cost.

Halloran walked out of the alley the way she'd come in—unhurried, alone, already thinking about the next one.

Behind her, the pharmacy sign swung once in a wind that hadn't been there a moment before, and was still.
